items.title: AWS Challenger: Trainium3 Inference and Microarchitecture Deep Dive
items.content:
The Nvidia GPU was originally built to shade pixels, and every Nvidia generation since 2017 has bolted on another piece of AI-specific hardware to fix the bottleneck the previous one exposed. Volta added Tensor Cores, Hopper added TMA for tile data movement between HBM and SRAM, and Blackwell added Tensor Memory for accumulating. Nvidia removed many hardware units that are required to render graphics for their datacenter GPUs
 In comparison, the Trainium microarchitecture is built ground-up specifically for ML workloads, with tiles as a first-class primitive instead of having a sea of threads and then bolting on tensor/tile compute and data movement engines. Trainium3 behaves the way the physics says it should. In this past this meant software was a humongous challenge, but now no longer.

 Source: Dwarkesh Podcast 
 7 months later, Trainium 3 and TPUs are live on InferenceX , both trading blows or even winning vs Nvidia GB300 in cost to generate tokens at TCO. We will dive into those details below.
 This advantage is not purely due to Amazon’s ultra low cost supply chain. It's also due to microarchitectural decisions, which we will dive into in this post. For example, using the Trainium Descriptor Generation Engines (DGE), the equivalent of Nvidia TMA and AMD MI455X TDM, our microbenchmarks show that Trainium can reach peak HBM bandwidth utilization (MBU) at small message sizes, which is not possible on Nvidia GPUs.
 Furthermore, our testing covers cycle-level SRAM scratchpad latency and bandwidth testing (SBUF to PSUM), rack-scale bandwidth and latency microbenchmarks, attention exponential testing, and the precise cycle-level latency of different shapes, including how different attention head_dim (K) would affect the percentage of roofline.
 Every result comes from UBenchX, our microbenchmark suite, and we model each unit from first principles before we measure it. We thank Nafea Bshara (Co-Founder of AWS Annapurna Labs), Ron Diamant (Trainium Chief Architect), Michael Shteinbok, Armin Ebrahim and the rest of their team for helping teach us their architecture and validate our benchmark experiments.
 Star the InferenceX & UBenchX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful ! InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and now, Trainium3.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Trainium’s Superior Inference Performance per Dollar - AgentX AgentX measures Trainium3 on a production end-to-end agentic inference workload. This is achieved by replaying real coding-agent sessions against a Trainium3 server. The goal is to compare accelerators’ realistic inference performance, that you may expect to see on actual agentic workloads.

 For those unfamiliar with InferenceX, the Pareto frontiers (curves) represent the fundamental inference tradeoff between throughput and latency. Each point is a different inference configuration targeting a different latency-throughput target. At each slice of the x-axis, higher perf per TCO is better and directly leads to higher inference gross margins.

 Today, we are excited to share that Trainium 3 PDS + vLLM achieves amazing perf/$ TCO across the entire frontier. In fact, it is better than every other accelerator besides Vera Rubin across the entire TCO versus p90 interactivity curve. This is an amazing achievement. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Trainium is also very competitive from an end-to-end latency perspective, across the entire curve. With that being said, there is still room for improvement, particularly with respect to TTFT.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 It is not surprising that Trainium lags behind in some p90 TTFT cases against GB300 as this metric is largely dictated by prefill, a compute bound operation. Trainium3 has only 17% the theoretical FP4 flops as Blackwell Ultra (2,517 TFLOPS versus 15,000 TFLOPS). It has more competitive interactivity since decode is memory bound and Trainium3 has 4.9 TB/s per chip against 8.0 TB/s for GB300, 61% of the bandwidth at about 30% the TCO. Also, pipelined prefill (which Trainium relies on, as discussed in the subsequent section) generally favors throughput over latency.
 In fact, at a p90 interactivity of 135 tok/s/user (a typical speed you’d observe on OpenRouter), Trainium3 with vLLM yields the highest profit margin at 73.5%, compared to runner up GB300 + SGLang at 53% (at 3 year rental prices). This assumes Z.ai list price for token pricing and a 60% hardware fleet utilization factor.
 Trainium3 achieves these margins with 144GB of HBM per chip, half GB300’s capacity per GPU. This reflects our Short King thesis: additional HBM capacity must deliver enough extra throughput at the target latency to justify its cost. This is also why 4-Hi is attractive industry wide option and next generation accelerators are primarily using 8-Hi.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 What makes these results interesting for this article is how directly the software follows the hardware we measure in Section 2. Prefill and decode run on separate nodes, and each arranges the same 16 chips to suit the topology.
 Prefill A quick primer for this section: a Trainium3 chip has 8 NeuronCores, each pair sharing one HBM stack, and a node is 16 chips. Section 2 covers the hardware in detail. For a more in depth analysis, see our Trainium3 deep dive article.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 A prefill node is a pipeline. The model’s layers are cut into 16 stages, one chip per stage, and a chunk of prompt tokens flows from chip to chip. Inside a stage, the chip’s 8 NeuronCores split the chunk between them, so all of the stage’s tensor and expert parallelism stays on one chip.
 This is the layout our collective benchmarks argue for. Chip-level collectives were well ahead of every wider group we tested, and all-to-all, the pattern MoE layers need, is slower once it leaves the chip. With the heavy exchanges kept on one chip, what limits a stage is TensorE, which is where the MXFP4 matmul modes covered below do their work.
 Decode 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 For decode, one copy of the model is spread across individual ranks on all 128 NeuronCores (across 16 chips), and every core takes part in the computation for each token. For those familiar with Nvidia architecture, each GPU is typically a separate rank whereas Trainium treats all 128 cores as logical devices and separate EP ranks. In the case of multi-user GLM-5.3, this assigns two routed experts per NeuronCore. Decode runs at LNC=1, so each physical NeuronCore is its own rank, whereas the rest of this article uses the default LNC=2.
 Again, each NeuronCore is its own device with local HBM, so nothing synchronizes across the chip unless the software invokes a collective. Nvidia added locality domains in CUDA 13.4 to pin Rubin kernels to one die’s memory in the same way.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Not every exchange spans the node though. Decode declares nested groups of cores: half a chip, one chip, the two chips of a tray, two trays, half the node, and the whole node, plus a second family that takes the same core position on every chip. The smaller exchanges, such as the dense layers and the shared expert, can run on the small groups. A group of 8 is one chip and a group of 16 is one tray, whose two chips share a direct link, so those exchanges never touch a switch. But activations are gathered across all 128 cores and the expert outputs are reduced across all 128, so that traffic crosses the switch on every layer.
 Trainium Profiler Fine-grain Accuracy - Better Than Nvidia and AMD Trainium’s profiler is by far the industry leader and is state of the art (SOTA). Trainium’s profiler is loved by all the performance engineers at Anthropic. Anthropic’s head of performance has publicly said that performance analysis on Trainium is way better than performance analysis on Nvidia GPUs (and obviously better than on AMD GPUs). In order to demonstrate how fine-grained their profiler is, we recreated the Olympic performance of the Bay Area’s own Alysa Liu on the actual Trainium3 hardware profile. We were mainly inspired by the Bad Apple post from Daniel Liu (Anthropic Performance Engineer). This combines fine art, performance art, and chip architecture all into one video.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Full video: 

 Section 2: Microbenchmarks Hardware and Programming Model Trainium3 consists of 8 NeuronCore-v4s, and every 2 NeuronCores share an HBM stack. By default, 2 NeuronCores that share an HBM stack form a Logical NeuronCore (LNC). Users write kernels that map to LNCs, and in LNC=2, it follows the Single-Program Multiple-Data (SPMD) paradigm: NeuronCores in an LNC execute the same kernel program with separate hardware resources except the HBM. In a Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) kernel, programmers can assign work to NeuronCores in an LNC with the API nl.program_id and synchronize NeuronCores with the barrier mechanism nisa.core_barrier.
 One of the most important concepts in data movement is the partition dimension (pdim) and the free dimension (fdim). Every tensor has a designated partition dimension, and other dimensions are called free dimensions. In principle, the partition dimension aligns with the dimensions of hardware components, and data can be processed in parallel. We explain the dimensions of each component throughout the article.
 Memory HBM Bandwidth Here we investigate the achievable HBM bandwidth of Trainium3. In Trainium3’s memory hierarchy, we move data from HBM to SBUF using the API nki.isa.dma_copy . Each NeuronCore comes with 16 main Direct Memory Access (DMA) engines, in charge of moving data between HBM and SBUF. For every data transfer, a main DMA engine ingests a DMA descriptor, which contains the source and destination address information. In Trainium3, there are three modes of generating DMA descriptors: static (None), software-based DGE (swdge), and hardware-based DGE (hwdge). Each mode generates and stores descriptors differently.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Starting from NeuronCore-v3 (Trainium2), GpsimdE comes with one integrated DMA engine per processor, totaling eight integrated DMA engines. With these integrated DMA engines, programmers can perform data movements in parallel with the main DMA engines, while also enabling indirect access patterns, such as gather and scatter operations. NeuronCore-v3 also comes with two Descriptor Generation Engines (DGE) . DGE accelerates descriptor generation with hardware: it frees up GpsimdE to perform other computation, frees up memory space, and accelerates address generation. DGE resembles Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) in Nvidia architecture and Tensor Data Mover (TDM) in AMD architecture. TMA focuses on accelerating large data copies at the cost of higher latency, while hardware-based DGE has no performance trade-offs compared to software DGE. However, while TMA is able to perform gather and scatter operations, not even the latest NeuronCore DGE can do so. As a result, NKI constrains DMA copy mode to swdge when performing indirect memory accesses.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Here we compare the achieved memory bandwidth of a single Trainium3 NeuronCore for the three descriptor modes. Static mode, since descriptors are compiled ahead of time, has the lowest descriptor generation overhead and achieves the highest memory utilization. At the smallest tested message size 64 KiB, static mode achieves 492 GB/s (80% utilization) for load and 544 GB/s (88.8% utilization) for store. Static mode also achieves near peak memory bandwidth at around 256 KiB. Hardware DGE, the default mode of DMA copy, follows closely behind static mode: it achieves 398 GB/s (65% utilization) for load and 476 GB/s (77.7% utilization) for store at 64 KiB message size, likely due to the address generation overhead. The gap narrows as message size increases, and hardware DGE mode matches static mode after 256 KiB. On the other hand, software DGE performs significantly worse than the other two. This likely indicates indirect memory access patterns may suffer great performance loss, as they are restricted to software DGE mode.
 Trainium3 consists of 8 physical NeuronCores, and while they have individual DMA engines, each pair of NeuronCores shares one HBM stack. Thus, we measure the memory bandwidth achieved by 8 concurrent NeuronCore programs to understand the utilization under full load. Overall, the HBM is able to sustain the high utilization, dropping by only about 3% for larger message sizes.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 PSUM to SBUF Bandwidth In Trainium3, PSUM and SBUF are arranged in a 2D grid of 128 lanes of 16 KiB / 256 KiB capacity. The 128-lane setup is the partition dimension, and the data is accessed in parallel along the partition dimension.
 There are two main types of data movement between PSUM and SBUF:
 SBUF to PSUM: Upon an nki.isa.nc_matmul call, TensorE moves both input matrices from SBUF to PSUM
 PSUM to SBUF: Epilogue operations such as data type casting, activation, and quantization. These operations are mostly based on the nki.isa.tensor_copy API
 This section focuses on PSUM to SBUF. Two engines have PSUM read access: ScalarE and VectorE. We measure the achieved memory bandwidth for the two engines across different tile shapes, using the full 128 partitions with varied per-partition sizes.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Our results show that PSUM read bandwidth starts from 453.9 bytes per cycle for ScalarE and 413.9 bytes per cycle for VectorE at 32 KiB message size, and both reach near the theoretical bandwidth of 512 bytes per cycle (4 bytes per cycle per lane, 128 lanes) at around 256 KiB message size. This translates to a 614.4 GB/s bandwidth for each engine. Starting from NeuronCore-v3 (Trainium2), the two engines can perform PSUM reads in parallel. Our benchmarks show that parallel access causes near-zero bandwidth loss, indicating that the PSUM is well designed to sustain parallel access. When both engines are used in parallel, they reach 1024 bytes per cycle.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The bandwidth gap between the two engines in the smaller message sizes indicates different instruction issue overhead: ScalarE has about 8 cycles of overhead, whereas VectorE has about 16 cycles.
 Tensor Engine Tensor Engine (TensorE) is the hardware unit that executes matrix multiplications. In terms of architecture, TensorE is a systolic array, which consists of a 128-by-128 processing element (PE) grid. The 128 dimension matches the number of partitions in SBUF and PSUM, and since TensorE reads both matrix inputs from SBUF and writes the results to PSUM, this simplifies programming. TensorE applies near-memory accumulation: the output accumulates in PSUM, avoiding a round trip to HBM, and it is especially useful for epilogue operations and consecutive matrix multiplications. This design is also present in Nvidia Blackwell, where the TensorCore output accumulates in TMEM.
 We invoke TensorE with the API nisa.nc_matmul . For a matrix multiplication of x @ y = z, the input dimensions are as follows:
 Stationary x.T: [K, M]. Maximum of M (stationary fdim) is 128; TensorE reaches full performance at K=128
 Moving y: [K, N]. Maximum of N (moving fdim) is 4096. This is because PSUM has 16 KiB per partition, which can hold a maximum of 16384 B / 4B = 4096 FP32 elements
 Output z: [M, N]
 Note that TensorE requires the stationary matrix x to be transposed, meaning the hardware takes x.T as input but computes x @ y. This is due to TensorE’s systolic array design: the systolic array computes dot products between rows of x and columns of y.
 Simple Systolic Array Performance Model In the systolic array, each y column is staggered by one element. Every TensorE matrix multiplication involves two steps: LoadStationary (LS) loads the stationary matrix into the array, and MovingMultiply (MM) performs the calculation. During each cycle of MM, every PE computes a partial sum, passes the y element to the PE on its right, and passes the partial sum to the PE below.
 Trainium3 systolic array performance model animation. Source: SemiAnalysis

 With the understanding of the systolic array, we can model the instruction latency as N+254 cycles. In a matrix multiplication, the lower-right element is the last to complete computation, and it depends on how many cycles it takes to move the lowerleft element of y into the lower-right PE. Focusing on the dynamics of the lower-left element of y, we see there are three stages: fill, stream, and drain. The fill stage refers to the period when the input edge isn’t full due to staggering, which is R-1 cycles, where R represents the number of rows in the PE grid. The stream stage refers to the last row entering the PE grid, and it takes N cycles for the lower-left element to reach the input edge. Finally, the drain stage is when the PEs consume the moving matrix inputs, and it takes C-1 cycles for the lower-left element of y to get to the lower-right PE, where C represents the number of columns in the PE grid. Overall, the latency is (R-1)+N+(C-1)=127+N+127=N+254 cycles.
 We can also model the initiation interval as approximately N cycles for sufficiently large N. Initiation interval is the time gap between instruction launches when we consecutively launch many of the same instructions. In this case, we model the number of cycles between a series of MM instruction launches. From the perspective of the systolic array, we can continuously stream multiple input matrices y1, y2, … in the same staggered fashion, and the computation of the next MM instruction starts as soon as the next input matrix’s element streams into a PE. In a steady state where we ignore the fill and drain stages, each PE streams through one row of input matrix y for every MM instruction, meaning the initiation interval is N cycles. However, this only holds for large N due to our steady-state assumption.
 nisa.nc_matmul Performance We collect experimental results to verify our modeling. We are able to map the latency results to the formula N+393 with little error, indicating that there’s a roughly 140-cycle overhead for MM instructions, which may include things like writing results to PSUM.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 As for the initiation interval, experiments show that by adding a constant 6-cycle overhead, we are able to reliably predict the initiation interval for matrix multiplication shapes N >= 64 and M=128. As we suspected, the model breaks down for small N, and we observe the initiation interval to be 30 cycles at N=8, likely dominated by other overheads.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Our model also predicts that M is irrelevant to both performance metrics, and our experiments corroborate this. At N=512, both latency and initiation interval stay constant across all M sizes. This has great implications for performance. LLM inference decode workloads tend to have small M for matrix multiplications, and M not being the main factor in performance alleviates many difficulties when optimizing decode workloads.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 We also measure a more realistic scenario, where we change both stationary and moving matrices, so the kernel alternates between executing LS and MM instructions, and the two instructions of different matrix multiplications can overlap. Results show that we reach more than 90% utilization at N=64, and we reach near theoretical throughput for shapes larger than N=128.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Double FP8 Matmul Performance Starting from NeuronCore-v3 (Trainium2), TensorE supports FP8 matrix multiplication. In terms of programming, users set the argument perf_mode to nisa.matmul_perf_mode.double_row, and double row mode supports contraction dimension K=256, 2x the standard K=128. However, the systolic array is still a 128-by-128 PE grid, so under the hood, double row mode shards the input into two tiles along the K dimension and computes them in parallel. items.title: Evaluating Recent Model Releases on GDPx
items.content:
Earlier this month we released GDPx , a benchmark designed to measure the domains most valuable for frontier intelligence. Most agentic benchmarks only measure a single domain like coding or legal. The few that try to be comprehensive, like GDPVal or Agent’s Last Exam , make the mistake of selecting domains based on percentage of GDP or the O*NET taxonomy.
 AI’s impact is nowhere near evenly distributed across the economy today, and we expect this trend to intensify in the future. Many tasks already can’t justify paying for Fable 5.2, much less Fable 7. Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. 
 It’s for this reason that GDPx intentionally forgoes industries like government and real estate, and instead covers the following domains:
 Chip design
 Cybersecurity
 Biology
 Finance
 Legal
 Quant trading
 Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
 Hardware design
 Materials science
 Alignment
 Software engineering
 Our methodology is also unique. To ensure all our tasks are truly representative of their respective domains, we partnered with 14 specialized data partners to make 206 tasks.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 The single most notable thing about GDPx, however, is its difficulty. Whereas other benchmarks will often debut with the top model scoring over 50%, Opus 5.5—the highest-scoring model on release day—scored just 12% on GDPx. This massive headroom is what allows GDPx to discriminate between future model releases, unlike saturated benchmarks such as Terminal Bench 4.0 .
 Speaking of new model releases, it’s been a very busy month indeed.
 SemiAnalysis is hiring for GDPx! If you’re interested in helping cement GDPx v2 as the world’s best benchmark, reach out to gdpx@semianalysis.com. 
 A flurry of new model releases Since launching GDPx on November 1st, both Anthropic and OpenAI have released new frontier models. Google made a dramatic resurgence with the Gemini 4 series, and we’ve seen notable releases from Alibaba and Moonshot as well. The GDPx leaderboard now looks like this:

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment, the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in, and switch to partial grading to get more signal from the extremely difficult legal and finance domains (which default to binary grading), we get the following leaderboard instead.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 We think you can argue either of these is the “correct” GDPx leaderboard. On one hand, safety classifiers truly limit the usefulness of models in domains like cyber and bio. On the other hand, if the goal is to measure a model’s intelligence, penalizing it for refusing to attempt a task due to safety concerns feels quite unfair. As an aside, we did find that 6.2 Astra’s classifiers are weaker than 6 Astra’s, but the model itself will refuse to do tasks that 6 Astra’s classifiers previously blocked.
 Either way, OpenAI is the current king of GDPx . Going off the main leaderboard, which covers all domains, 6.2 Astra ranks first with a score of 19.3%. Fable 5.2 ranks second at 16.4%, and the best non-OpenAI/Anthropic model, Gemini 4 Carbon, ranks fifth at 10.9%. Carbon just barely edges out the highly lauded Gemini 4 Neon, which ranks sixth with a score of 10.1%.
 The cost-performance Pareto frontier is also entirely dominated by OpenAI. DeepSeek v4.1 Flash just barely sneaks in at the very low end.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 Although the Twitter hive mind has recently been dumping on 6.2 Astra and praising Gemini 4 Neon, we believe GDPx accurately captures the true relative ranking of model capabilities in frontier domains. This will become clearer as we break down overall scores by domain in later sections, but Astra and Fable remain decisively above all other models in terms of raw intelligence . It’s just that most Twitter influencers simply aren’t working on hard enough problems today to truly push frontier models to their limits, which is why we believe Twitter vibes are more a reflection of how pleasant models are to work with, rather than raw model IQ. We agree that OpenAI’s newest round of models is extremely unpleasant to work with, much like that 1 autistic coworker who is just so cracked everyone deals with their bullshit. We attribute this to OpenAI RLing the model extremely hard and very far while having poor SFT data.
 Gemini 4 Neon Gemini 4 Neon is the model of the moment, with some declaring it the single best model in the world.
 Earlier this year, we published a newsletter predicting the demise of Gemini/DeepMind. Clearly we were wrong. Compared to their competitors offerings at the time, Gemini 4 Neon is much better than Gemini 3.8 Flash was, and model progress at DeepMind has inflected up over the past few months. Neon is the best at Bio, but likely because OpenAI and Anthropic have more refusals.
 With that being said, the GDPx results show Gemini is still decisively behind both Anthropic and OpenAI across virtually all frontier domains .

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 6.2 Astra significantly outperforms Gemini 4 Neon at RSI, materials science, and hardware design, while Fable 5.2 dominates in chip design, software engineering, and quant trading. Neon is the top-scoring model in biology, but this is likely due to more lenient safety classifiers (though we did find Neon to have stricter safety classifiers in cyber than other Google models).
 We believe Gemini 4 Neon’s overwhelmingly positive reception is largely due to model behavior and not intelligence. Put simply, Neon is a pleasant model to talk to. Its liberal use of exclamation marks and cheerfulness reminds us of GPT 4o, which was a similarly adored model.
 In terms of the overall AI race, we believe Anthropic and OpenAI are still clearly in a tier of their own. Google is a distant third, but also deserves its own tier. Meta, SpaceX, Moonshot, Alibaba, etc. are all fighting for 4th.
 Lastly, as we previously explained to Tokenomics Model subscribers, it’s worth noting that Neon is unnecessarily expensive to run because Google’s prompt caching lags behind its competitors. Running Neon on GDPx cost us $15,286. Had Neon matched Opus 5.5’s cache hit rate, that bill would have been $12,536, about 18% less. At 6.2 Astra’s cache hit rate, it would have been $10,403, about 32% less. We compare theoretical cache hit rates here, meaning the share of cacheable input tokens that were actually served from cache, since that isolates the quality of each provider’s caching stack from how a particular workload is structured.
 To its credit, Google shipped a caching update just today (another 4.5% increase to Neon’s cache hit rate, which would cut this bill by roughly 17-18%), so some of this gap may already be closing. Improving an inference serving stack is also something models are rapidly becoming superhuman at, so we expect this gap to continue closing in the near future.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol GPT-6.2 Astra and 6.2 Sol both do extremely well on GDPx, scoring 19.3% and 11.5%, respectively. Interestingly, this goes against most people’s subjective impressions of the models. Public reception to 6.2 Astra on X was embarrassingly bad , with one influencer calling it the “worst model OpenAI has ever released.”
 However, 6.2 Astra also represents a significant drop in base model log-perplexity, which OpenAI recently disclosed as one of the best proxies for measuring models pretraining intelligence, and therefore sample efficiency. How do you explain this apparent contradiction?
 Taking a closer look at individual GDPx domains reveals the answer. GPT-6.2 Astra excels on tasks that require complex reasoning like chip design, hardware design, materials science, and RSI. It’s also the first model to score higher than 0% on legal, and it is SOTA on finance.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 Notably, 6.2 Astra is lackluster at software engineering, which is the domain most people on X evaluate models on. It scores half that of Fable 5.2. Qualitatively, the model is also often too literal when following instructions, fails to infer user intent/make reasonable assumptions, and is just generally annoying to talk to. Most users aren’t working on science problems hard enough for 6.2 Astra to flex its genius, so it’s no wonder why public sentiment was generally poor.
 Interestingly, we did observe some examples of 6.2 Astra having a very good understanding of industry norms for particular domains. As an example, it knows that before adding an acquisition to a buyout model, you check whether anything the company has signed since the model was built changes the numbers. On one of our M&A tasks, it searched the data room for every document dated after the model it was given and found a signed letter that changes a payment the company already owes. That was the first correct answer any model has produced on that task.
 It’s also worth emphasizing that 6.2 Astra scores extremely high on alignment. It appears that OpenAI’s safety commitments post Hugging Face weren’t just for show, and it’s reassuring to see such rapid progress here.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 6.2 Sol is similarly spiky to 6.2 Astra and worse at everything except quant and SWE. Overall, we believe the current negative sentiment around OpenAI’s models is overblown. The 6.2 series is clearly extremely smart, and OpenAI completely dominates the cost-performance pareto frontier as well—they just need to do a better job making their models pleasant to work with.
 Fable 5.2 Fable 5.2 is the second-best model on GDPx at 16.4%, behind only 6.2 Astra, and the gap narrows once safety classifiers are taken out (29.9% vs 32.2% with partial grading). It’s also by far the most expensive model to run. At $88 and 1.23M output tokens per task, Fable 5.2 costs 1.9x as much as 6.2 Astra and uses 3.9x as many output tokens, for a lower score. 
 Much of this comes from Fable 5.2’s increased persistence and its proclivity for spawning subagents for testing and review. For now, all GDPx runs are done at the highest possible reasoning level.
 Materials science is the starkest example. Fable 5.2 costs 2x as much as 6.2 Astra per task and uses 3.7x as many output tokens, yet scores 19 points lower (21.8% vs 41.3%). Even 6.2 Sol beats it (25.8%) at roughly a tenth of the cost ($8 vs $79 per task).

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 Finance tells a similar story. With partial grading, Fable 5.2 scores 53.6%, effectively tied with Opus 5.5 (54.6%) and 6.2 Astra (53.5%). But it uses 2.3x as many output tokens as Opus 5.5 and 12x as many as 6.2 Astra, which makes it 6.6x as expensive as 6.2 Astra per task.
 Software engineering is where Fable 5.2 shines. At 24.4%, it nearly triples Opus 5.5 (8.9%) and is well ahead of the next best model, 6.2 Sol (15.6%). Even here the extra capability isn’t free: compared with Opus 5.5, its cost per task rises by about the same multiple as its score (2.8x), and it costs 17x as much as 6.2 Sol.
 It’s also interesting to note that 6.2 Astra does significantly better than Fable 5.2 at RSI (33.22% vs 24.13%). However, we think this is largely due to Anthropic explicitly nerfing their public models’ AI research abilities.
 Qwen4-Max and Kimi K3.1 Pro Qwen4-Max is the highest scoring Chinese model on GDPx at 7.44%. It’s a little worse than Claude Sonnet 5.5, though significantly cheaper. Qwen4’s biggest gains vs Qwen3.8 are in software engineering, RSI, cyber, and bio.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx 
 Kimi K3.1 Pro performs comparatively worse on GDPx than other benchmarks like the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , but this is largely because K3.1 Pro is benchmaxxed on Terminal Bench 4.1 (which is 10% of the AA index). K3.1 is unironically the number one model on Terminal Bench, when in reality, the model clearly still lags Fable 5.2, Gemini 4 Neon, 6.2 Astra, etc on agentic coding.
 We believe GDPx provides the most accurate relative ranking of model quality and continue to be pleasantly surprised how well the benchmark matches our subjective opinions.
 We’d also like to thank Modal for being our inference provider for Kimi K3.1 Pro.
 Custom cyber post-trains As part of this update, we also evaluated a number of custom cyber models. It’s clear that domain specific models are becoming significantly more relevant as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google continue to crackdown on their safety classifiers. Speaking from firsthand experience, it is extremely non-trivial to get unmitigated cyber/bio access from any of these providers. We believe this is a good thing for the safety of the world, but it also means that from here on out, the majority of users will be better off using models from different providers for these select domains.
 Furthermore, Anthropic is also explicitly nerfing capabilities like RSI, and there are other domains like materials science where having proprietary data can enable non-frontier labs to train state of the art models. We plan to continue evaluating many more domain-specific models on GDPx in the future. 
 We tested 3 custom models on GDPx cyber
 A cyber post-train of DeepSeek v4.1 Flash from Hinoki called HO1
 Abliterated versions of Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash from Boundless 
 Surprisingly, the 2 abliteratred models performed slightly worse than their vanilla open source counterparts, while Hinoki HO1 performed marginally better.

 Source: SemiAnalysis GDPx

It will be interesting to see whether custom models can demonstrate stronger GDPx performance in the near future with additional post-training.

items.title: Nvidia and the World Without Jensen
items.content:
Jensen Huang is no longer the CEO of Nvidia . Nvidia’s board was investigating Jensen’s conduct and weighing his future at the company he founded, and clearly the conduct issue is real; it is ethically problematic to have relationships with a customer who is a Chinese CCP asset and with multiple subordinates.
 Additionally, we believe there is more at play with his resignation after only four days. We believe it is directly tied to the vast smuggling of GPUs. Our Accelerator Model tracks every AI chip’s production and destination, and our data shows more than 1.5GW of Nvidia chips, which are restricted, still ultimately ended up in China. This figure doesn’t even include chips that Nvidia created to circumvent US rules, a story we originally broke .
 We believe the US intelligence community is a large part of the push to get Jensen out of Nvidia. Specifically, we believe it is likely that RASA or similar legislation, which has already passed the house, will move forward. AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone. We are strong believers in some restrictions, but poorly shaped ones are damaging to US interests.
 This sort of legislation will have consequences, and we don’t think politicians are thinking them through.
 Here are the clear benefits of the current regime where Chinese labs are able to access GPUs remotely, and NOT in China:
 Profits flow to American companies.
 The US can monitor what Chinese labs are doing.
 The US can cut off their access to the GPUs through politics or by force almost instantly, if they choose.
 American companies such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Supermicro, and Dell all depend on Chinese companies in their supply chain.
 American companies such as NVIDIA and AMD employ Chinese engineers (who live in China, to be clear) to develop hardware and low-level software for their GPU systems. Without these engineers, we are certain that the user experience for these GPUs would be materially worse than it is today.
 American companies, especially the entire startup ecosystem benefit from the open source research that Chinese companies, students and independent researchers publish using these GPUs today.
 China is (even slightly) less motivated to use their domestic accelerators.
 Innovations from China flow globally through open innovations of wide expert parallelism, OSS kernel libraries: MSA, DeepEP, DeepGEMM, etc.
 With that said we do believe in some AI restrictions to China, but those are more shaped like the MATCH Act then RASA. Biden style diffusion rules make the most sense.
 Maybe biggest of all: open source is under attack . It’s an open secret that Nvidia works directly with the Chinese labs on open source and helping them optimize GPUs and models. These labs utilize Blackwell GPUs, which Nvidia knows. The US open source ecosystem and many startups rely on Chinese AI models. This is significantly impaired with Jensen gone and the China hawks winning.
 But the question that matters for shareholders (and the AI supply chain) is a different one: what is Nvidia without Jensen?
 Our view is that the company was never built for him not to be there. He was at the helm for 33 years, and even though the board pressured him out (or he “resigned”) Nvidia would still be materially better off with him there instead of gone. The company was uniquely built to suit the man himself. The company without the man might be an entirely different beast. SpaceX and Tesla don't function without Elon, Nvidia doesn't function without Jensen.
 One King, 60 Direct Reports Nvidia’s corporate structure is odd for a company of its size and scale. Jensen has roughly 60 direct reports, according to his public statements. He has said that CEOs should have the most direct reports because those people require the least amount of management and that he doesn’t have one-on-one meetings with them.
 But few of them can do things without Jensen. The company is run like a kingdom with one king, with everyone else, regardless of seniority, a peon doing his bidding. Jensen has said that it doesn’t matter who reports to who as their title isn’t related to how important their job is, and it’s one of the reasons why Nvidia is the “smallest large company in the word” and has so much fewer employees – about 42,000 – despite its big market cap. At Nvidia, there is less politics as a result. Jensen has said this flat network empowers employees and allows the company to adapt more quickly because its technology is also moving so quickly.
 This is one of the reasons Nvidia moves fast. Once Jensen set a direction, everyone moved on it together. Former employees have told us that product development and engineering often happen until the last minute so the company can change its mind if it needs to. For example, the GB200 design came together a lot closer to the product cycle than probably anyone would have liked, one former executive told us. Jensen has said he wishes he could keep the company in startup mode forever.
 The cost of that structure, however, is that Nvidia doesn’t have a deep bench of successors. Look at Nvidia’s website: only five others, two of whom are legal and finance executives, are featured prominently among his reports. Most of his direct reports aren’t trained for the spotlight and are actively discouraged from seeking it. Few leave to become CEOs of other major companies, with Rene Haas at Arm the rare exception. Few at Nvidia get the chance to shine externally because Jensen makes all the big decisions. But much of Nvidia’s executive team doesn’t mind because heavy is the head that wears the crown, and many are happy to stay until retirement age because they’re well paid, treated well, and believe in the mission and their leader.
 No One Wants the Job Colette Kress has been named interim CEO, but Nvidia is looking for a permanent CEO. That cannot be someone with finance background. The obvious internal names being floated to succeed Jensen on the technical side are Ian Buck and Jonah Alben. Buck, who created CUDA out of his doctoral research at Stanford, joined Nvidia in 2004 and now runs the datacenter business as vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. He is often placed in charge of things while Jensen travels and frequently speaks at conferences.
 Alben, who has been at Nvidia since 1997, is senior vice president of GPU engineering and oversees the design of the company’s GPUs. But realistically, no one person can run it all. We don’t think Buck is capable of running the technical hardware engineering side of the house. Alben and others on his team have technical autonomy, but even he doesn’t control the entire chip side, where other senior leaders who handle many major technical and business divisions also report directly to Jensen. Both are amazing but likely not able to exert the supply chain mastery Jensen has.
 There is also the question of whether anyone wants to do the job of CEO. An executive told us earlier this year that “Ian would rather die than succeed Jensen and wouldn’t want that job. Jonah is more respected and people say he could, but again, no one would really want that job.” Circumstances, though, have obviously changed. Kress is the interim CEO, but wrangling more than 60 VPs to a cohesive vision of the company takes a certain kind of person, and otherwise the firm’s direction risks dissolving into noise.
 Founder Bets Do Not Survive Professional Managers Jensen is one of the last old-school tech founders, of the same generation as Elon Musk and a bit older than Mark Zuckerberg. The other companies that came up alongside Nvidia have all transitioned to professional managers, including AMD, Google, Microsoft, Apple and Amazon.
 Nvidia’s success relies on big bets that can take years, if not a decade, to pay off. A founder with the full support of the board can take those risks without worrying about a revolt. CUDA lost money for years while Wall Street analysts kept questioning it, but Jensen held steady and the bet paid off enormously. As one former employee put it: “Jensen put the whole company behind programmable shaders, CUDA and tensor cores despite a lot of opposition to spending transistors on them when use was limited.”
 Omniverse and autonomous driving are the new bets within Nvidia. Internally, Jensen calls them “zero billion dollar bets,” former employees tell us. They make no money today, but he sees them as just as big as CUDA. He also built the Shield TV consumer entertainment box and the DGX Cloud service on the idea that Nvidia needs to understand its customers to design better products, even if those two businesses made little or no money and were ultimately cast aside.
 An Nvidia successor who isn’t the founder, no matter how long they have been at the company, answers to the board and shareholders in a different way. Long-term bets and convictions of this kind become much less likely, and one of the biggest issues is Jensen’s legendary kingmaking and dealmaking, which is going to be hard to replicate.
 Customers Bought Jensen, Not Just GPUs Jensen was the chief decider on chip allocation to the hyperscalers and everyone else. Customers are always jockeying for allocation and fighting for Nvidia’s attention, and more and more of Nvidia’s deals require extensive Nvidia support. As we wrote in July , Nvidia has a choice over whether to allocate more capacity to hyperscalers, neoclouds or neoclouds on its backstop program, where it credit-supports the cluster and takes a share of the cloud revenue. This central bank of Nvidia was backed by the full faith and credit of Jensen. The next CEO is unlikely to be able to make the bold bets Jensen did.
 Nvidia likes to decide based on what’s feasible, but much of it comes down to what makes strategic sense. It doesn’t always make strategic sense to skip the hyperscalers, or to work with them and treat them preferentially. Many of these customers now need reassurances that they will continue to be supported by Nvidia through financial guarantees or allocation. Nvidia disclosed $530B of gross off-balance-sheet guarantees as of its fiscal second quarter, up from $184B the prior quarter, including $36B of take-or-pay floors under neocloud capacity, and it holds a $99B equity book.
 Many customers also want a deal with Jensen for reasons that go beyond the numbers. Neoclouds around the world raised their money because Jensen backed them, not because they compared chips and chose Nvidia. Nvidia’s backstops let neoclouds and neolabs raise money without the hyperscalers: it sells GPUs at full margin on day one, then floors the buyer’s revenue, guarantees the buyer’s landlord or signs the lease itself, so that operators without an investment-grade rating can borrow at investment-grade pricing. If the Jensen put is not there, there might be a large contraction in this ecosystem.
 The Supply Chain Stranglehold Loosens Nvidia has a stranglehold on its suppliers. If competitors had access to supply, they would ship much higher volume. They can’t get it because Jensen has personally locked up memory in South Korea and chips in Taiwan. As we wrote in The Great AI Silicon Shortage , Nvidia has locked in most of the supply for logic wafers, memory and various other necessary components, and Jensen’s 2025 trip to Korea was to secure memory supply, before other executives quite realized how in shortage memory was. Our industry clients thought our forecasts for 2026 were too aggressive, but then they realized we were right . Nvidia’s supply and capacity commitments jumped from $119B to $279B in a single quarter, primarily for memory.
 That stranglehold is personal. Jensen was the one who won these deals, CEO to CEO, with the major supply chain companies around the world. In Korea, we estimate SK Hynix’s 2027 HBM4 pricing could range from roughly $3.0 to $3.3 per Gb for Nvidia versus $3.7 to $4.1 per Gb for other Tier 1 customers including AMD, Broadcom, Amazon and Google, and we believe there is an implicit understanding that Nvidia gives SK Group priority GPU allocation in return. Without him, these firms will no longer prioritize Nvidia to the same degree, and capacity will be easier for others to acquire. We think it’s likely that in 2028 more than 70% of total capacity could be non-Nvidia. 
 What’s more, beyond strangling the supply, Jensen’s vision is what pushed the supply chain in Taiwan to invest harder and believe more in this buildout than anyone else. Jensen’s legendary supply chain dinners and commitments are what pushed suppliers in Taiwan to deliver on technologically and logistically aggressive plans.
 The AI Industry Loses Its Open Source Spokesman Without Jensen, the AI industry loses its chief spokesman. He was everywhere, speaking on AI as its chief proponent. He was the face of AI, and no one can replace that.
 Jensen also set Nvidia’s China policy and led its push for open source AI models, which give countries, enterprises and neoclouds a reason to buy GPUs beyond the handful of frontier labs, who are now building their own chips.
 As we wrote in September , no one needs open source AI more than Nvidia: it is on track for a world where it has only two real customers, Anthropic and OpenAI, or seven including the hyperscalers, and all seven except SpaceX are trying to build their own XPUs to cannibalize Nvidia’s margins. AI models and applications are the complements to its GPUs.
 It is an open secret that Chinese frontier labs use Blackwell GPUs & NVIDIA DevTech collaborates closely with the Chinese frontier labs & learns a lot from their end users, which results in innovations to the CUDA ecosystem like wide expert parallelism, DeepGEMM, DeepEP etc. These then spread to the western open source community and startups. These startups are massively negatively impacted by the departure.
 Without Jensen being the spokesperson and offering financial and engineering help for open models, Chinese labs may not be able to open source kernel libraries like MiniMax MSA, DeepGEMM, DeepEP, Moonshot’s FlashKDA, which are clearly targeted at NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Many production engines used widely across the world like SGLang & vLLM use these innovations from Chinese labs. Chinese labs may have to go back to straight up denying that they have any NVIDIA GPUs and keep their NVIDIA software internal only instead of open sourcing Blackwell software.
 This is fundamentally bad that innovations from China won’t be shared across the NVIDIA ecosystem & the general ML ecosystem anymore. It is positive for closed AI labs but bad for startups.
 A manager lead company could depriortize underperforming Nemotron , With many models going closed source at the frontier labs in the U.S., Nvidia was single-handedly propping up the other American open source models with its efforts by investing in firms like Reflection, Thinking Machines, Poolside, and the Hugging Face acquisition.
 Nvidia was the one pushing continuous engagement with China, on the argument that China should use and rely on American technology. As we wrote last year , after the U.S. government banned the H20 from going into China and then indicated Nvidia would be granted a license to export it, the U.S. needs to balance having China on the U.S. AI stack and slowing the development of its own, while also limiting the quality and volumes shipped into China. Now, what if he was pushing it from a compromised place? That is up to the investigation to figure out. Clearly the China hawks are winning, so we have to ask a bit of an odd question. Why now?
 Why Now Does Jensen’s Personal Life Come to Light? We aren’t ones for conspiracy theories, but a few events around the same time seem to create a narrative that is hard to ignore. The intelligence community had much to gain. The second New York Times story on the topic explicitly states (five times) that the basis for its reporting is the U.S. intelligence community. Trump, Rubio and Lutnick have known about all of this since before their trip to China in May. What’s more is that there is reporting that Lutnick stalled the Chinese chip crackdown . Something has shifted in that relationship, and now the wind is blowing in the other direction.
 We actually don’t believe Alice Huang is a spy in the traditional sense. She is a well connected business woman. She like any other well connected business person in China, has contact with the CCP. 
 Our Accelerator Model has tracked over 1.5GW of Nvidia GPUs that shouldn’t be in China, The Department of Commerce now also finally believes that there is more than 1.5GW of NVIDIA chips in China that shouldn’t be there. Now, with the midterms swinging the Democrat’s way, someone has decided it is time to put the hammer down both to stop the willing circumvention of the existing export controls and to expand them to cut off China’s access to frontier chips once and for all.
 To be clear, the Trump administration is split on the issue, but Trump was giving Lutnick cover. Trump is no longer providing that cover. What’s more, there is a critical bill called the Remote Access Security Act (“RASA”) that has passed the House that has yet to receive a vote in the Senate, and that vote is happening right now.
 RASA Up for a Vote RASA passed the House 369-22 on Jan. 12. It passed on a motion to suspend the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority. The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved it 51-0 in April 2025. Though it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, it hasn’t yet received a vote. We know that NVIDIA and Oracle have been lobbying against it, hard .
 Of course, RASA isn’t the only way that the U.S. government can stop Chinese companies from accessing GPUs remotely. But RASA is the bill that is the hot topic of discussion in Washington right now. It is clearly popular, having already passed the House, and the substantive portions of the bill seem downright obvious to people. Why allow Chinese companies to access GPUs remotely that they aren’t allowed to import?
 For what it’s worth, we are aware of neoclouds in Asia, Australia, the Middle East, Nordics, Europe, Canada and even the U.S. that are actively selling capacity to Chinese companies. All of them would be impacted by this bill. This is another global export control bill, and one with far-reaching implications. Jensen, and likely Lutnick, did not want this to happen.
 So let’s go against the popular narrative and explore the possibility that despite all of the recent headlines, passing RASA (or something like it) will have unintended consequences . To follow the old adage about American politics, we believe that if all the politicians agree on something, it’s probably a bad idea.

items.title: We Visited China’s Stargate in Inner Mongolia
items.content:
Stargate Abilene has become the symbol of America’s AI buildout. It is a gigawatt-scale campus on the Texas plains built for OpenAI. China has campuses on a similar scale, though few people outside the country have had a look inside. In September, we visited one, and we found the speed, scale, ultra low cost, and deep vertical integration astonishing.
 During the trip, we toured Inner Mongolia, China’s fastest-growing AI datacenter region. It's the “West Texas” of China, but while the Lone Star State faces its highest ever anti-datacenter sentiment, Inner Mongolia is accelerating and faces no such backlash.
 Our main stop was Galaxy, a campus in Ulanqab planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity. 
 Galaxy is about the size of Abilene’s core campus. Its first 120MW phase was delivered within a year at a fifth of US costs. All four phases are built-to-suit for two internet giants. 

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 When we visited, the rest of the campus was still a busy construction site, and the surrounding Chahar High-tech Zone had nearly 30,000 construction workers on site across 22 datacenter projects according to a local report. As we noted in our primer on the China datacenter market , with this much labor available, Chinese datacenters rarely take a fully modular approach, yet construction costs keep falling. We take a closer look at why in this report. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The datacenter is owned by Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator with more than 100GW of wind turbines installed worldwide. It came to datacenters from energy management, a path many others are taking today. Yet it is one of the most vertically integrated players we have ever seen. 
 Beyond running the datacenter, Envision builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply it. Its blade factory sits just across the road from the Galaxy datacenter campus, with finished blades stacked in the yard. 
 Inside the campus, it designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V system, manufactured the battery storage that smooths the load, and co-designed the prefabricated substation.

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 In one 5MW hall, we saw the 800V system at work. Solid-state transformers (SSTs) take 10kV AC from the grid and convert it straight to 800V DC for the racks. This removes the low-voltage transformers, UPS and rectifier stages in between. The same architecture is still on the US roadmap, as we outlined in our 800V DC deep dive .
 In China, datacenters have been running on DC power for almost two decades, from China Telecom’s 240V DC pilots in 2007 to Alibaba’s Panama power system in 2018. Today, roughly a quarter of Chinese datacenters built in the past decade run on DC, while about 97% of US datacenters still use AC UPS. An SST is a natural next step on that path, and we cover the evolution and the pilot in detail later in this report. 

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 On cooling, Galaxy uses a design common in Inner Mongolia. Liquid- and air-cooled servers share one water loop, with no central chiller plant. Nvidia says Vera Rubin can run on 45°C water without chillers, yet most datacenters in the US keep one for air-cooled equipment and for the flexibility to shift between the two. Galaxy drops the central chiller and keeps much of that flexibility, a design that has been running at scale in northern China for years.
 In this report, we use what we saw on the site visit to show how China builds hyperscale datacenters today, with a deep dive on each of the topics above. Many questions still open on the US roadmap find a reference point here. 
 Our next report will take a wider view of Inner Mongolia’s datacenter market. The region has lined up 25GW of announced datacenter projects, including several gigawatt-scale campuses. Many reports picture it as a land of empty datacenter halls. Our data tells a different story. Few have asked what limits datacenter development there. We look at each constraint, from power to land and water. Stay tuned. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model This trip was part of our ongoing fieldwork for the SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model , the China counterpart to our global SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model . 
 It tracks over 1,000 facilities across 70+ operators, with quarterly delivery curves through 2032, a lease signing and delivery tracker, and EDWC hub and cluster analytics. Every project in our report is tracked in the model. 
 Contact sales@semianalysis.com for more information.
 SemiAnalysis is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support our work, consider becoming a subscriber.

 China’s Stargate campus Envision comes to datacenters as a renewable systems integrator. Beyond building wind turbines, it designs, integrates, and manages power systems across the full chain, from generation and storage to computing loads. Its affiliate, Envision AESC, develops and integrates batteries, energy storage systems, and the power electronics and software that link them.
 Inner Mongolia has far more wind than its existing industry and population can use, so policy encourages bringing new demand to where the renewable resources are. In Chifeng, Envision built a 2GW off-grid wind, solar and storage system that feeds a green ammonia plant. The system runs entirely on power electronics, with no synchronous generator. A small pilot datacenter built with Tencent’s modular T-Block units runs on the same system. Galaxy is a larger application of the same idea. 
 This is a pattern we see across China right now. Industrial groups with an edge in energy, construction or electrical equipment are pivoting into AI infrastructure. Project returns are thin, with IRRs squeezed hard, so the reward often comes from elsewhere. For Envision, datacenters create new demand for the power and equipment it already produces. For many listed companies, the draw is the stock market. 
 Of these newcomers, Envision is one of the most ambitious. Its datacenter plans in Inner Mongolia add up to 3GW. Galaxy is the first. Its initial phase was delivered in August 2026, and the full campus is expected to be completed by the end of 2027. 

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The scale of the campus invites comparison with Stargate’s flagship campus in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe began building Abilene in mid-2024 and leased it to Oracle, which runs it for OpenAI. Crusoe describes the eight-building campus as 1.2GW of power, which comes to about 820MW of critical IT capacity, on par with the 800MW planned at Galaxy. That makes Galaxy one of the largest single campuses in China. Our SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model also tracks an expansion phase that Crusoe plans to add, powered behind the meter, which takes the whole Abilene site to 1.5GW of IT capacity. Galaxy also has room to grow. If the wind turbine factory next to the campus is converted, a later expansion phase could take the campus to ~1GW.
 In addition to scale, the two share a starting point. Both are developed by companies with roots in energy, and both were planned around their own power. Abilene draws on the grid and on gas turbines on site, while Galaxy relies largely on wind. 
 What sets Galaxy apart from Abilene, and what draws our attention, is its vertical integration. 
 Own wind for its own load Galaxy’s power comes through a model China calls source-grid-load-storage (”SGLS”). Under this model, a project builds its own wind and/or solar farm, battery storage and datacenter, and links them through a dedicated line instead of the public grid. 
 For hyperscalers, the appeal of an SGLS project is long-term power at a largely fixed cost. Power from wind and solar also counts toward green targets.
 Inner Mongolia holds about 57% of China’s usable wind resources. A wind farm here runs on average about 2,800 full-load hours a year, a capacity factor of roughly 32%. Ulanqab is windier, with a capacity factor of 35–40%. That sets the starting point for how much of an SGLS project’s power can come from wind.
 For Galaxy, Envision aims to supply over 60% of the first two phases’ power use with its own wind farms. Three factors make this possible:
 Siting. Envision chose windy sites, even though they sit about two hours’ drive from the campus. The two wind farms are about 80km apart, which cuts the hours in a year when neither has wind.
 Scale. The wind farms have a combined 420MW of installed capacity, about 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load. With this oversizing, even light-wind hours can still cover much of the load.
 Storage. A 4-hour battery storage system shifts power from windy hours into calm ones. Most SGLS projects add storage too, but Envision makes its own storage systems and runs them on its own software, which we detail in the next section.
 The chart below shows how each factor raises the wind share, using illustrative curves. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 Panel 1 starts with a simple case: 1MW of wind for every 1MW of datacenter load. A good site in Ulanqab produces as much power in a year as running flat out for about 3,500 hours. To keep it simple, the panel shows the farm at full output for 3,500 hours and at zero for the rest of the year. Wind covers 40% of the year’s power.
 Panel 2 shows a more realistic picture. Wind output goes up and down, so the panel sorts every hour of the year from windiest to calmest. The farm is the same size as the load, so it never produces more than the campus uses. All its power gets used, and wind still covers 40%.
 Panel 3 doubles the wind farm. Output in every hour doubles too, so even light-wind hours now cover much of the load, and wind’s share rises to about 55%. The cost shows in the gray area. In windy hours, the farm produces more than the campus can use, and that power must be stored or curtailed.
 Panels 4 and 5 show what can be added on top. A 4-hour battery moves some surplus into the hours after the wind drops, though it cannot help much when the wind stays calm for days. Better matching between wind output and load can push the share even higher. 
 The table at the bottom shows how the result changes with wind quality, the size of the wind farm relative to the load, and how fully the datacenter is used.
 Inside the campus: developer, designer and integrator Beyond pairing energy production with consumption, Envision is also integrated inside the campus, acting as more than a developer and operator. The chart below shows its three roles, in three colors.

 Source: Envision, SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model 
 The first is as a manufacturer. Envision designs its own turbines and develops the converters and control software. The battery energy storage systems (BESS) at both the datacenter campus and the wind farm come from its affiliate AESC, which builds every major part in-house, from cells to power conversion and software, so the whole system can be tuned and tested together at the factory before shipping. Most vendors cover only one part of the system (high voltage, low voltage or generators), so getting the parts to work together falls to on-site commissioning, which can take 3–6 months. Envision’s factory pre-configuration has become its core selling point. 
 The second role goes beyond Envision’s traditional business into the datacenter space. For Galaxy, Envision designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V SST system. 
 800V DC is the architecture that Nvidia is pushing for its next generation of high-density racks, as Kyber racks at around 600kW cannot be served efficiently at today’s voltages. In the US, the industry is still early on this path. SSTs that convert medium-voltage AC straight into 800V DC are the final step. Galaxy’s SST pilot is only 5MW, but it already runs 800V DC all the way to the rack at a live hyperscaler site. We discuss this in detail shortly. 
 Lastly, Envision co-designed the prefabricated substation sitting inside the campus. The substation is built and tested as modules in the factory while civil work goes on at the site, then shipped and connected on site. This takes less than 3 months, versus about 6 months for a conventional indoor substation.
 Today, vertical integration on its own does not lead to hyperscaler orders, but two trends suggest it could matter more over time.
 First, access to power is becoming central to datacenter development. In the US, developers bridge the power gap with on-site gas turbines, fuel cells and batteries. In Southeast Asia, governments have been pushing developers to bring their own power this year. Malaysia now requires datacenters to source at least 30% of their power from renewables and encourages on-site generation. In China, approvals increasingly favor projects that pair compute with green power, under the national push for “Compute Power Coordination.” Across different markets, access to energy is becoming part of what a datacenter developer sells.
 Second, the power architecture from the grid connection to the rack is being redesigned. In the US, the industry is moving toward higher-voltage DC power, while battery backup units (BBUs) and BESS are starting to take over the role of UPS. The technology roadmap is not settled yet, but the shift looks set to continue, giving integrated players room to compete differently from traditional developers. 
 These trends have drawn other players onto a similar path. The closest case is the tie-up between VNET, CATL and Zhongheng Electric. 
 VNET is a leading colocation operator, CATL is the world’s largest EV battery maker, and Zhongheng Electric is China’s largest supplier of HVDC power systems for datacenters, working with both Alibaba and ByteDance. 
 In 2026, CATL became VNET’s largest shareholder and announced a deal to take a 49% stake in Zhongheng Electric’s controlling shareholder. It has since agreed with VNET to jointly develop gigawatt-scale datacenter campuses, and separately with Zhongheng to work on datacenter power systems. Between them, VNET covers the datacenter side, CATL leads green power and storage, and Zhongheng brings power conversion inside the hall. 
 CATL is also one of DeepSeek’s largest outside investors, which extends its reach downstream to the model layer. 
 Where Envision builds most of the pieces in-house, CATL links them through partnerships and equity stakes.
 China’s datacenter market is highly competitive. Rents have roughly halved over the past five years, to about $40/kW/month excluding power. Capex has fallen about 25% over the same period, to less than $3mm per MW. Power in Inner Mongolia costs about $0.055/kWh all-in, among the lowest in the world. 
 In a market like this, owning more of the value chain is one way to differentiate, a playbook familiar from China’s EV market, where players like BYD make much of what goes into their cars.
 It is too early to say whether vertical integration will become a meaningful advantage in China’s datacenter market. For now, it gives integrated players more control over cost and schedule, but hyperscalers still choose vendors mainly on resources and track record. That could change as power becomes harder to secure and the power system inside the datacenter is redesigned.
 Behind the paywall, we walk through how Galaxy was built and designed in detail. 
 On speed and cost, we follow Galaxy from land auction to customer acceptance and explain why capex keeps falling. 
 On power, we trace how China took a different path from the US, adopting 240V DC in its datacenters years ago, and walk through Galaxy’s live 5MW pilot. A larger version is planned for the next phase. 
 On cooling, we take apart a design common in northern China that offers one answer to the chiller debate in the US.
