items.title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
items.content:
In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported.
 Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy .
 Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300.
 We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading.
 Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX.

 Source: Dwarkesh (Dylan’s Cousin) Podcast 
 Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity.
 Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result:
 Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang).
 GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss.
 Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy.
 Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by vLLM OSS ecosystem developer, Inferact.
 This was benchmarked on InferenceX/AgentX, the industry-standard inference benchmark supported by almost every major buyer of compute, from Microsoft Azure to Oracle to Meta and many more. Furthermore, it has the support of the ML community, including vLLM, LMCache, SGLang, PyTorch, and Huggingface, and the support of major labs like OpenAI, MiniMax, ZAI, Qwen, Moonshot Kimi, etc.
 Google potential TPU customers and current TPU customers are asking Google for AgentX results because of how realistic the AgentX benchmark is and how similar it is to their real inference workload. For our SemiAnalysis supply chain shipment estimates on TPUv8i, TPUv8t, TPUv9, TPUv10, check our Accelerator Model for full quarter by quarter breakdown of shipments. 

 Source: InferenceX 
 Star the InferenceX GitHub repository if you find the open-source benchmark and data useful!. InferenceX is the only inference benchmark in the world to have TPUv7, OpenAI Jalapeño, Nvidia Rubin NVL72, AMD, and soon, SambaNova and Trainium2/3.

 Source: InferenceX 
 Recommendation to Jensen NVIDIA only occasionally loses to AMD on some model/scenarios , but TPUs delivering better performance per dollar or competitive performance per dollar is a new experience that NVIDIA senior leadership is unwilling to accept. As soon as TPU posted its first AgentX result on Qwen3.5 397B FP8 showing that even TPUv7 FP8 could beat GB300 NVL72 FP4, NVIDIA tasked a strike force of human engineers and agent swarms to work 997, late into the night until 2am local time and on weekends, across USA and mainland China. Unfortunately for NVIDIA, their first GB300 FP4 counter submission is still 1.64x worse per dollar than TPUv7 FP8 for external customers across most of the curve. We do think that with enough agent swarms, NVIDIA could regain a slight performance lead on GB300 NVL72 FP4 vs TPUv7 FP8, but on NVIDIA FP8 versus TPUv7 FP8, we believe that it is not possible for NVIDIA to regain SOTA for certain models.
 One thing we hear a lot from open-source maintainers in PyTorch and NVIDIA customers is that there is a lot of bureaucracy; simple things, like adding a new feature to the NVIDIA driver to support a certain feature for PyTorch CudaGraph capture, have been stuck in “internal NVIDIA legal review” for three months. It makes little sense for lawyers to be the blocker for technical driver features. We have seen similar challenges when trying to get NVIDIA to add features like improving ConnectX, NVSwitch, HGX Board (Vulcan, Umbriel) DCGM power telemetry, where it takes a while just to get the timeline for the timeline. In comparison, startup mindset companies like AMD (under the leadership of Anush, Ramine, Vamsi, Lisa) can rapidly develop these features.
 There needs to be an cultural shift in massively reducing bureaucracy at NVIDIA. This is one of the biggest risks to NVIDIA Moat that Jensen has to tackle. In our experience and many customers experience, Nvidia is now slower moving than AMD, Google, and Amazon to external suggestion, git commits, and feedback. 
 That being said, certain teams at NVIDIA are cutting through the bureaucracy, such as the NVIDIA ex-CentML vLLM team . AMD and TPUs added innovative Megakernel decode support to open source popular production inference engine . Within a week, they were able to defend the NVIDIA by rapidly adding and merging Megakernel support too (PR approved by AMD vLLM maintainer). 
 TPU is making big headway into the ecosystem, and multiple models, like Day 0 Meta’s Muse Spark Open support and Kimi K3.1 Pro already has day 0 TPU support , as it applies the NVIDIA playbook of giving open-source maintainers lots of chips. In contrast, NVIDIA’s contribution of clusters to community maintainers has increasingly been wrapped in DMV style bureaucracy and stingy at best. For a $5 trillion company, one would expect NVIDIA to be more liberal in contributing resources to OSS developers who work for free on improving the NVIDIA stack. We hope Jensen figures out how to eliminate the bureaucracy slowing progress. 
 In comparison, AMD has been increasingly less stingy and providing the upstream vLLM, TileRT, SGLang, Tokenspeed, etc. maintainers liberal access to clusters and rapdily increasing the CI fleet without miminal levels of bureaucracy.

 Source: vLLM Dashboard 
 Meta’s Muse Spark Open FP4 816B on SGLang TorchTPU Agentic Inference Performance Meta is one of the early adopters of TPU and is already deploying TPUv7 in production using SGLang-TorchTPU.

 Source: Meta 
 Muse Spark Open is Meta’s latest 816B-parameter open model, and it is one of the launch models for SGLang-TorchTPU. On InferenceX’s agentic inference workload, a submission from RadixArk, a community developer and a lead maintainer of SGLang, shows that TPUv7 is competitive for decode performance per dollar even when using the cost basis of what Meta would pay when buying TPUs. For production inference, Meta uses SGLang for LLM inference and uses vLLM for RL training rollouts. When looking at end-to-end latency, TPUv7 still needs improvements to be competitive, such as continuing to optimize its prefill kernels. For decode kernels, TPUv7 SGLang is using a fully fused megakernel, which eliminates kernel launch latency. Furthermore, the submission uses SGLang HiCache CPU DRAM offloading using Google’s open-source, TPU native TPU-Sync library at high concurrency in order to improve prefix cache hit rates.

 Source: SemiAnalysis & RadixArk 
 Note that Muse Spark Open is an extremely GPU-optimized model, and, in theory, not friendly to TPUs at all. This is due to Muse Spark Open’s 64 head dim, which means that for long-context attention, 25% of the systolic array is padded.
 In comparison, GPU matrix cores consume small tiles, so a wide range of head dimensions, expert widths, and post-sharding KV head counts all land near peak. A dimension of 64 instead of 128 pays close to nothing on an H100 or a B200 and gets a cheaper attention layer for it. GPU architecture allowed researchers to prioritize evaluation performance without a loss in inference performance.
 This is quite interesting as TPUs can get quite competitive performance on a model that is extremely unfriendly to TPUs. Note that AI labs with lots of TPU capacity, such as Anthropic and Google Deepmind and soon OpenAI, typically co-design their models such that the attention shapes would fit nicely on TPUs to avoid this issue.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 When TPUs see model architecture with attention head_dim=256, they go full lambo mode.

 Source: Mario Kart 
 Great work to the RadixArk team on this amazing achievement! They are actively working on updating the documentation such that everyone can get access to this optimized SGLang Muse Spark Open TPU configuration. We expect more AgentX results from RadixArk soon, showing that its SGLang-TorchTPU stack is production-ready.
 GLM5.2 / 5.3 vLLM AgentX FP8 Agentic Inference Performance GLM-5.2/5.3 is a frontier open model. It is an MoE transformer with 744B parameters and roughly 39B active per token. The model supports a 1M-token context through DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): a lightweight indexer scores prior tokens, and full attention runs over only the 2,048 selected tokens for each query.
 For FP8, TPUv7 is the cheapest way to serve GLM-5.2 AgentX. From 60 to 300 tok/s/user, it delivers 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X at FP8 , and 4.4x that of H200 at 150 tok/s/user.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 FP4 GPUs Still Lead on Perf per Dollar Because GLM-5.3 was not natively QAT with block scale FP4, FP4 has a slight accuracy drop compared to FP8. FP4 GPUs still deliver more tokens per dollar at most speeds, as TPUv7 has no native FP4 support, and we will need to wait until Q1 2027 for TPUv8 with FP4 support, as tracked in our Accelerator & HBM Mode l. At 100 tok/s/user, GB300 and GB200 FP4 deliver 3.6x and 3.5x the tokens per dollar of TPUv7. FP4 halves the bytes per weight, and small batch decode is memory bound.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The SemiAnalysis AI Cloud & TCO Model provides a comprehensive breakdown of pricing across all accelerators currently on InferenceX, as well as many more, including future SKUs such as Nvidia Rubin Ultra and Feynman, AMD MI400 through MI700, Google TPU v8 through v12, and AWS Trainium3 through Trainium6.
 Get Access 
 GLM-5.3 Optimizations GLM-5.3 AgentX contexts reach 1M tokens with over 90% of each request already cached, so KV cache capacity sets how many users fit. There are four main changes:
 GLM-5.3’s attention reads one shared compressed KV entry per token, so splitting attention heads across devices would copy the whole cache to every device. Decode context parallelism (DCP) splits it by sequence position instead and merges partial attention results every layer.

 Source: SemiAnalysis & Google 
 Each query reads only the 2,048 cache entries an indexer selects. TPUv7’s SparseCores, built for scattered memory access, pick those entries and gather them while the TensorCore runs the attention math.
 TPUv7 uses registers that are 8 rows by 128 lanes. Data must be packed into them, which can fragment. The 128 indexer key bytes plus the scale byte add up to 129, one byte more than a 128-wide row, so the old layout rounded it up to 256. The new layout turns it sideways: tokens now run along each row, and each token’s key runs down 32 four-byte rows, plus one more row for the scale. That comes to 132 bytes, and only 3 of them are wasted.

 Source: SemiAnalysis & Google 
 One fused kernel runs routing; the experts, the all-reduce, and the attention merge become a single collective. TPU programs are compiled for fixed shapes, so Google added 4- and 8-token shapes for small decode steps, which had been padded to 16.
 Qwen3.5 397B AgentX Two weeks ago, Qwen3.5 397B became the first model Google submitted to AgentX. Its TPUv7 FP8 vLLM results on our agentic inference benchmark demonstrate that it is 1.67x better perf per dollar than even FP4 GB300 NVL72.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 NVIDIA may try to claim that it doesn’t care about the Qwen3.5 397B model, but from analyzing our upstream InferenceX submission analytics datalake, the reality is that NVIDIA has spent over 20% of the sweep GPU hours on Qwen3.5 for certain NVIDIA GPU SKUs so it is hard for NVIDIA to claim that. In addition, if you look at the NVIDIA engineers assigned to Qwen3.5, it is some of the top 10x inference performance engineers at NVIDIA in mainland China and USA, so clearly, NVIDIA cares about optimizing this model.
 Furthermore, certain major hyperscalers/AI lab use Qwen3.5 397B and multi trillion parameter scale up version based on Qwen3.5 397B architecture as proxy models when making hardware purchasing and capacity planning decisions. So, this is a very important model for certain token factories.
 For readers making purchasing decisions, our AI Cloud & TCO Model extends the analysis into cluster economics, including cash flow, investment returns, and accelerator residual values.
 Get Access 
 AgentX captures the four elements of an agentic workload:
 Multi-turn: a session includes many user / assistant interactions (tens or hundreds) compared to a handful in a chatbot scenario.
 Long context: system prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns make context accumulate quickly.
 High prefix reuse: since the conversation progresses linearly, where output from turn n-1 is concatenated to turn n
 Sub-agent bursts: a session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, which create bursty KVCache patterns.
 TPU was able to demonstrate that its upcoming TorchTPU vLLM stack can successfully handle agentic workloads.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 NVIDIA First Counter Submission NVIDIA engineers worked overtime to launch their counter submission FP4, which beats TPUv7 FP8 on decode performance, but there is a slight issue: they overtuned decode at the expense of prefill, hurting overall end-to-end performance. Thus, on end-to-end performance, TPUs FP8 is currently still beating GB300 NVL72 FP4.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 

 Open Source Kubernetes llm-d puts TPUv7 far above GB300 FP8 for Decode Interactivity Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate hosts so long prefills do not stall generation. llm-d is the open-source K8s router that coordinates them, each host is 4 TPUv7 chips, and each result uses 24-32 chips.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Speed comes from capping how many requests each decode host runs, from one at a time at the low-latency end up to 112 at the high-throughput end. Requests over the cap wait for a free host, which adds to their TTFT. Even so, p90 time to first token at the fastest point is 8.6 seconds, against 11.1 for GB300 FP4’s fastest point.
 This uses llm-d, one of the largest ecosystem-based production inference kubernetes orchestrators. During the recent Kimi K3.1 Pro launch, they had Day 0 support for TPUv7 on llm-d .

 Source: InferenceX 
 At FP8, TPUv7 with llm-d beats GB300 at every interactivity, from >2x at high throughput to achieving more than 1000tok/s/user in the ultrafast region.
 Unfortunately, using this turn-based routing algorithm does lead to worse end-to-end performance for TPUs compared to GB300 TRTLLM FP4. However compared to FP8 and FP4 GB300 NVL72 SGLang, it is still much better.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Qwen3.5 TPU Optimizations Qwen3.5-397B mixes 45 linear attention layers, which keep a fixed-size state per request, with 15 full attention layers. Google describes three main changes:
 Decode megakernel. One kernel runs the whole decode step and prefetches the next layer’s weights while the current layer computes.
 Host DRAM offload. KV cache and linear attention state spill to host DRAM through TPU Sync, Google’s newly open-sourced offload framework.
 Cache-aware routing. llm-d sends each turn to the prefill host holding its prefix and keeps each session on its decode host unless that host is full. Google says routing to the exact data-parallel rank raised decode cache hit rates from 56% to 76%.
 Kimi K3 AgentX TPU from Inferact and AMD shipped megakernels for frontier MoE models first in open source engines. NVIDIA quickly followed within a week with its own megakernels.
 A conventional decode step launches hundreds to thousands of kernels, and the chip idles between them. A megakernel runs many layers in one long-running kernel that prefetches the next weights, while the current ones compute. AMD calls its version the MonoKernel. On GLM-5.2 across eight MI350X GPUs, AMD reports that it cuts a decode step from about 2,459 launches to 210 and runs 2.31x faster at batch 1.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 A megakernel removes the idle gaps between kernel launches. Read more about megakernels in our TileRT article:

 For this setup, DCP was used for prefill. The prefill and decode variants of context parallelism describe where each technique usually helps, not where it can run. K3 uses MLA which stores KV as one latent shared across heads, so TP cannot split it and every TP rank holds a full copy. DCP fixes this by giving each TP rank a different slice of tokens. Prefill context parallelism would have needed a lower TP degree, which copies weights onto more chips and leaves less HBM for the KV cache, already the scarce resource here.

 Source: Inferact 
 Competitive with GB300 FP4 at launch At launch on October 17, TPUv7 delivered 0.77x to 0.91x GB300’s tokens per dollar from 50 to 200 tok/s/user and was 1.6x faster for a single user, at 391 tok/s/user against 251. On Google’s internal cost it beat GB300 at 100 and 200 tok/s/user.

 Source: InferenceX 
 GB300 FP4 now leads by 1.5x to 2.6x after four NVIDIA refreshes. TPUv7 still delivers a competitive 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200 and B300, while VR200 delivers 4.3x to 5.6x TPUv7.

 Source: InferenceX 
 In an apples to bananas comparison between TPUv7 & Rubin NVL72, Rubin is up to 6x better perf per dollar. But note that this is an unfair comparison as Rubin should be compared to TPUv8i which we will be benchmarking very soon.

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 It is important to note that Rubin’s results remain preview submissions . We look forward to NVIDIA providing direct Rubin access so we can independently reproduce these results and run the full InferenceX/AgentX suite.
 Built by the Ecosystem This result came from the vLLM ecosystem, not from Google alone. Inferact, founded by vLLM’s creators and maintainers, built the K3 megakernels with Google, and the two submitted the result together. The megakernel plugs into vLLM as a model runner that replaces only the forward, so vLLM’s scheduling, prefix caching and KV transfer work unchanged. The stack is open source on vLLM TorchTPU, and Inferact’s reproduction guide runs it from a Docker image. Ecosystem development like this has mostly happened on CUDA.

 Source: Inferact

items.title: Elon Is Doing It Again: SpaceX Will Be The World’s Biggest AI Cloud
items.content:
We wrote at length about how SpaceX’s plans for 10GW in 2027 was feasible , paving the way for 300b+ ARR. We received a lot of pushback from folks calling it impossible. Now, just two months later, we’re already seeing 3.6GW under construction across multiple sites, both existing and new . SpaceX has even revised its estimate up to ~13GW in 2027. This would be the largest amount of datacenter capacity ever built by any one company in that timeframe, roughly equivalent to all of Google’s datacenter capacity from 1999-2026 in just 1.5 years. We think it’s possible and have already identified >9GW of capacity. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 We’ve since written multiple update notes to our Datacenter Industry Model subscribers showing off all the sites that can make this possible. We now believe that SpaceX may be the fastest datacenter builder in the world , even more so than Chinese peers . Watch how Colossus 2 adds nearly two Stargate Abilenes (2GW) in just under one year!

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 These sites now build so fast that the power supply is often identified mid-flight. Looking at our Energy Model , we see that power under Elon’s management (>8GW) is less than our total datacenter power coming online (>9GW).

 Source: SemiAnalysis Energy Model 
 Datacenter Industry Model subscribers knew all of this before anyone else. On June 23, we sent our customers information on the infamous Elon “10GW in 2027” statement on SpaceX’s first earnings call by six weeks, pointing out a 5-10GW incremental order for 2027 was floating around the supply chain and that a new building was already under construction at Colossus 2, now publicly known as “MiniHard.” On September 14, before a single datahall went vertical, we identified >2GW of fresh sites , both at Colossus 2 and SpaceX’s Starbase campus.

 Starbase, Texas, October 29th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The Elon locations have a pioneering track record with us. We called Colossus 2 the first gigawatt datacenter in the world back in September 2025, when onsite gas was called a science experiment . We showed exactly how xAI bypassed the grid (and permitting!) with truck-mounted turbines, why the behind-the-meter playbook was going to spread to 40GW+ of behind-the-meter datacenters by 2028 , and how the Anthropic and Google deals turned SpaceX into the most profitable neocloud on earth . Now, Colossus 2 could soon house the largest BESS deployment in the world, with 5.9GWh already being installed, and more to come. 

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 This report unveils our analysis of SpaceX’s “proprietary plan.” From repurposing Starship’s rocket building and launching campuses into datacenter sites, to the gargantuan BESS deployment , buying out homeowners to house construction workers, and relocating mobile turbines, this report covers it all.
 For example, did you know TeraFab , Elon’s 100M sqft, 10GW+ chip fab project in Texas, will likely also have a datacenter? See the clip below of SpaceX representatives talking to Grimes County officials.

 Source: Local Filings
 Keep reading to find out why we think the TeraFab datacenter will be for third party renting!
 Subscribe now 
 And beyond the paywall, we dive deeper into the likely SpaceX power solutions, another site that may house a datacenter, and potential pricing for future SpaceX contracts, build off our proprietary SpaceX Funding Model as part of our Capital, Compute and Markets model. 
 Fastest Build Times In The World What does building two Stargate Abilenes in one year look like? Let’s talk about the Colossus expansions, where Elon is already trying to buy hundreds of nearby homes to both soothe noise complaints and provide construction worker housing . We’ve already spoken about MiniHard in Memphis finishing construction in just ~5 months, but the newly purchased “Gun Range” plot just south of the state line in Mississippi will take ~4 months!

 “Gun Range,” Colossus 2, October 28th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 To our knowledge, this would be the fastest greenfield datacenter ever built at scale. While most are fighting for 8-12-month build times, SpaceX has cut them in half.
 Looking closer at Colossus 2, we see SpaceX trying to break its own record again. SpaceX’s first retrofit at Colossus 1 took 122 days for 150MW, and Colossus 2 took just 91 days for 210MW. Now, SpaceX has taken the building (codenamed Project SPAM) directly in the middle of Colossus 2, and targets December to bring its first tranches online. With a construction start date of October 5, 2026, this could be shorter than the 91-day record, which itself broke the 122-day record; both are held by SpaceX.

 “Project SPAM,” Colossus 2, Mississippi, October 28th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model ; Note the Megapacks and Chillers already being deployed! 
 Colossus expansions were to be expected, but repurposing sites from Elon’s other ventures was not. For example, many are familiar with Elon’s Starbase in Texas, traditionally used for rocket building and launching. However, as flagged two months ago to Datacenter Industry Model subscribers , this site will now house two datacenters too!
 The site went from simply clearing ground at the end of August to full vertical construction by the end of September, and we now believe it will actively fit out datahalls in the coming weeks.

 Starbase, Texas, October 29th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 At this size, and with the knowledge of a 2027 timeline (meaning Vera Rubins), this site could be well over 1GW! Looking at the datacenter on the right, you can see that the steel mainframe is being built, while the roofing is actively following behind it. And on the left, you can see the transition from dirt to full preconstruction. These are multiple construction processes performed simultaneously, a visual representation of speed.
 Lastly, we have medium-high confidence that TeraFab will have a datacenter too. That’s right, the 10GW, 100M sq.ft chip fab venture from SpaceX will likely have a datacenter. We flagged this possibility ~3 months ago, and again 1.5 months, to Datacenter Industry Model subscribers, solely by examining preconstruction work and filings.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The project actually initially started as a datacenter and then quietly pivoted to TeraFab.

 Source: Local Filings 
 We showed the clip at the beginning (August 2026) of the site housing compute; furthermore, the representatives do not confirm that the datacenter will be for SpaceX’s use only, leaving room for third parties to rent the capacity too.

 Source: Local Filings
 The main remaining question is whether the current work on the ground is for one or more datacenters or for supporting facilities for TeraFab (like onsite gas, Central Utility Plant, etc.). We lean toward a datacenter for now, but suspect the vertical construction is moving slowly to ensure their JETI agreements/permits are fully compliant; otherwise, they may be subject to the TCEQ pauses or other regulatory scrutiny. Preconstruction work is so early that these pads can be pivoted a number of ways if datacenter work is not granted.

 TeraFab, October 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 How Are They Building So Fast? One thing often overlooked is that the Elon companies are some of the best hardware companies in the world. We mentioned in our previous newsletter that their labor can run at 3k workers per GW thanks to their top-tier engineers. However, we also believe that Tesla is manufacturing modular MEP equipment, allowing SpaceX to deploy so rapidly.
 If SpaceX and Tesla can manage their global supply chains appropriately, their partnership can easily construct GWs with far fewer constraints than others. This is like Crusoe manufacturing their own Switchgear to skip lead times , but on a massive scale. Tesla will likely become more than a BESS merchant to SpaceX soon.
 Largest USA BESS Deployment, Turbines, and A Grid Connection? Now that we’ve walked through GWs worth of sites, how will they power them? So far, we track 8GW+ of likely behind-the-meter capacity for SpaceX . This includes deals such as FTAI, Solaris, and others that only our Energy Model subscribers get access to. We have discussed how SpaceX decides the power on the fly, and one amazing example is the new Starbase, Texas site, where APRs are being deployed just one month after vertical construction started!

 Starbase, Texas, October 29, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 The site may use >1GW of APRs, but judging by building size, this will not be enough. And looking at the (two!) pipelines underway, the site will likely have multiple GWs of power, and more turbines on the way. According to a TikTok with the Brownsville mayor, the site is building a fiber optic channel through the Port of Brownsville, as well as looking at leasing waterfront space (potentially for its own port). At such a massive scale, we suspect most of the temporary turbines from Colossus 2 will be relocated here.
 Next, let’s move on to Colossus 2, where the opposite is happening: a grid connection. According to TVA (the region’s utility), Macrohard (700MW) and MiniHard (450MW) have both requested service for their facilities. For now, we assume this grid connection services Macrohard and MiniHard in full.

 Source: Local Filings 
 We’ve already seen SpaceX building out the 500kV gas-insulated substation (GIS) to the left of MiniHard, which is scheduled to finish construction by December 31, 2026, and connect to the Freeport substation.

 SpaceX GIS Substation, October, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 This comes at the perfect time, as the turbines at the Southaven power plant must be shut down. The site can legally operate 2.7GW nameplate right now, but only 1.24GW nameplate by July 2027, due to the binding requirement signed July 30, 2026.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Energy Model , MDEQ 
 But the eagle-eyed reader may notice: after subtracting the ~1.2GW grid connection, we’re left with 1.3GW of compute… and 1.24GW of nameplate power generation… Recall, nameplate generation still takes a haircut on efficiency and derate , and IT MW doesn’t represent the full facility load . There could be a gap upwards of 300MW. How does this get solved?
 We think there are a few ways, and the Energy Model team will explore this power system in depth soon. But first: we think SpaceX has built the largest BESS field in the USA for a reason. With the BESS nearing 6GWh, we think the site will orchestrate gas and BESS to increase baseload, while the turbines cycle through charging them. If the datacenters are designed right (and our IT MW assumptions are correct), this could work. Given some clusters are customer-facing while others are for internal training, there could be an SLA uptime tiering to increase total capacity.

 Colossus 2, Mississippi, October 28th, 2026; Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 We suspect that with an ultralow PUE of ~1.10-1.15, variance in datacenter types (inference vs training, customer-facing vs internal usage), rack designs using less power (Project SPAM using half the fiber of others), and the oversized BESS, the project may still be able to cover a ~300MW shortfall.
 Beyond the paywall, we will further discuss the power situation, and how we think SpaceX economics could play out.

items.title: GDPx: Measuring Frontier Model Capabilities Across the Most Valuable Domains
items.content:
GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities.
 We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. 
 Specifically, we cover the following domains:
 Chip design
 Cybersecurity
 Biology
 Finance
 Legal
 Quant trading
 Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
 Hardware design
 Materials science
 Alignment
 Software engineering
 And intentionally forgo industries like government, real estate, and insurance.
 Interpreting the results GDPx is a true frontier-level benchmark: even the best model scores just 12%.

 Source: GDPx 
 It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead.

 Source: GDPx 
 We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available.
 We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin .

 Source: GDPx 
 We also generally observe meaningful spikiness across all leading models.

 Source: GDPx 
 Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0.
 Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes.

 Source: GDPx 
 The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely.

 Source: GDPx 
 It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. To explore the data yourself, checkout the official website .
 A collaboration with 14 specialized data partners Domain-specific benchmarks have gotten significantly better over the past year largely thanks to the rise of specialized RL environment startups. Yet OpenAI’s GDPval (along with its derivatives like GDPval AA v2.1 ) remains the most popular general purpose benchmark still reported on major new model release cards . This is despite being released over a year ago on September 25, 2025—an eternity in AI land. GDPval may have been marketed as a “knowledge work” benchmark, but agents weren’t really even a thing yet. This had a huge impact on its task design, and as we’ll later explain, makes GDPval woefully inadequate for evaluating today’s frontier models.
 Our goal with GDPx is to create the world’s best benchmark for general agentic capabilities. However, as soon as we started working on this project, it became clear why we’ve yet to see a worthy GDPval successor. Models like GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 are already pushing the boundaries of human knowledge. If you want to make a finance or cyber task these models can only solve < 20% of the time, you need real domain expertise to ensure the task is hard for the right reasons. Many popular benchmarks sidestep this problem by shipping tasks that are downright unfair . This typically manifests in a grader that checks for requirements impossible to infer from the task description or environment. For example, a coding problem may ask the model to fix a bug that a human engineer would agree has two valid solutions—one using “module A” and another using “module B”. However, a poorly designed grader may require the AI to use “module A” and unfairly give 0 reward when the AI chooses “module B”. Correct all such issues, and the benchmark often ends up being saturated .
 Making high quality tasks for a single domain you have expertise in is already hard enough—there’s a reason why labs are willing to pay $5k+ for a single high quality task. Finding one company with sufficient expertise in both AI evals and enough domains to make a broad-based GDP benchmark is downright impossible.
 To solve this problem, SemiAnalysis partnered with specialized RL environment startups for each domain:
 Chip Design ( Aria , Arcverex , Ergodex )
 Cybersecurity ( Arithmetic )
 Biology ( Latch Bio )
 Finance ( Living Context )
 Legal ( Chakra )
 Quant trading ( Third Moment )
 RSI ( Extrapolate )
 Hardware design ( Beautiful Machines )
 Materials science ( ValenceForge , Emulated )
 Alignment ( Fleet )
 Software engineering ( Datacurve )
 All partners were subject to a rigorous QA process we detail in the methodology section. For some domains, we had multiple partners who wanted to be exclusive and ran a process to select the one with the highest quality tasks.
 We would like to give a huge thank you to all of our partners for contributing to GDPx. They’re among the best vendors for their respective domains and it would’ve been impossible to create such a broad-based benchmark without their help.
 Additionally, we’d like to thank Fireworks for providing inference for all the open source models, Modal for providing the sandbox infra needed to run our tasks, as well as Abhijay Rana for helping source some of the partners and assisting with early QA.
 Problems with OpenAI’s GDPval To be clear, we believe GDPval was impressive for its time and was the first benchmark to evaluate AI on such a broad range of tasks. It’s not OpenAI’s fault that a benchmark created before the rise of agents does a poor job evaluating them today.
 Every GDPval task is precisely specified and non-interactive, with all the necessary context directly spoon-fed to the model in the prompt. Consider the following representative finance example below:

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 Attached to this prompt is a very plain, single-page PDF that gives the model even more context about the two projects.

 An actual document used for an OpenAI GDPval finance task. Source: OpenAI 
 From here, the model is asked to directly one-shot its task of writing a 15 page pdf to recommend one of the two options.
 Any real finance manager could point out dozens of reasons why this task isn’t actually representative of their day to day work, but we will focus on two main issues:
 Despite the task description itself being unnaturally wordy, the overall task lacks detail about the “two significant investment opportunities.” The model is expected to take nothing more than a ~500 word, high-level description of the two options and convert it into an “up to 15 page” pdf recommending one of them. As you’d expect, even OpenAI’s reference solution is mostly filler slop.
 Relatedly, the task simply lacks a realistic, rich environment. A human expert tasked with making a recommendation between two investment opportunities would do a ton of research first to gather information—searching through pdfs, excel models, emails, etc. This process of gathering context is a big part of what makes actual work difficult and is entirely missing from GDPval.
 This second point is extremely important to understand. Not including domain-specific, simulated work environments for each task is the single biggest issue with GDPval. Agents today have already progressed well beyond narrow, well-scoped tasks like “generate a pdf/excel file/word doc/powerpoint based on just this reference file attached below + a few hundred word prompt,” yet basically every GDPval task fits this exact shape. As for tools, the model is only given access to web search, a code interpreter, and libraries to modify PDFs, word docs, excel files, powerpoints, images, audio, and video.
 Besides not having environments, GDPval also has many other issues including:
 Graders are entirely rubric-based which is often noisy. Human expert inter-rater agreement was just 71% on the gold subset and their automated grader was even worse.
 Broken rubrics with vague criteria, incorrect standards, and sometimes downright wrong requirements.
 Incorrect golden expert solutions that are used as references for grading the model output.
 Tasks that depend on a previous point in time and now have broken links , outdated prices , etc .
 Every GDPx task includes a realistic environment In contrast, here’s an example finance task from GDPx contributed by Living Context :

 Source: SemiAnalysis 
 The task environment is seeded by a real transaction from Living Context’s enterprise network. In it, Bannock Capital (a PE fund) buys ~62% of Haverly Snack Company for $880M plus an earnout. Eakin Lowry is the sell-side banker and Marbury Kline is the accounting advisor. The environment consists of ~4000 anonymized files separated into four categories: Haverly’s virtual data room (VDR) and independent deal folders for Bannock, Eakin and Marbury (all fake names of course).
 Each task is performed from the perspective of Bannock, Eakin or Marbury. Haverly’s VDR is always loaded into the environment along with the appropriate deal folder. The specific example above is an accounting task that an associate from Marbury was actually asked to do in the real transaction. Unlike the GDPval task that spoon-fed all the relevant context to the model in the prompt, the AI needs to adeptly navigate a real ~2000 file deal room to gather the right context in order to successfully complete this task—just like a real human associate did.
 All of our other domains contain similarly rich environments. Cyber tasks are based on real zero days discovered by Arithmetic’s security engineers and include multiple running services in the environment. Material science tasks put the model inside simulated laboratories complete with battery cyclers, a catalyst reactor, a transmission electron microscope, and more. Hardware design tasks include live sessions of Siemens NX and test the model output on real AWS FPGA instances. These are just a few examples—we’ll cover each of our partners in depth later in the article.
 Our methodology for GDPx We started by selecting the domains we believe will be most accelerated by AI in the next 1-2 years. This is closely related to a demand model we’re building for Tokenomics subscribers which projects OpenAI and Anthropic revenue in 2027 and 2028.
 We believe it’s a mistake to build a benchmark for general agentic capabilities based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy because AI diffusion won’t be equally distributed and not all domains will need frontier intelligence . Thus, if your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they’ll be most impactful. 
 From there, we reached out to 30+ RL environment companies that have expertise in chip design, cybersecurity, biology, RSI, materials science, etc. Every potential partner was subject to the same rigorous agentic QA (quality assurance) process which checks for consistency, completeness, cheating, unfair verifiers, and much more. Our QA process was based on Andrew and Max’s previous experience co-founding an RL environment startup that sold data to multiple frontier labs. When we run this same QA process on popular benchmarks like Terminal Bench 4.0, it flags nearly 50% of tasks as broken. Of course, we also manually reviewed hundreds of trajectories to verify what our automated QA was flagging and to catch things that automated QA normally wouldn’t. We also perform failure mode analysis on our tasks to ensure our set is diverse and that even within a task, models fail for a variety of reasons.
 However, we are also well-aware that any QA system can be gamed given sufficient iteration. If a task only passes QA after 3-4 rounds of feedback, it becomes very difficult to tell whether the task actually became good, or if the provider simply tricked your QA process.
 For this reason, all partners were required to pass our automated QA first try with only minor mistakes at worst . Of course, if our QC flagged serious issues, we gave potential partners the chance to explain why we were incorrect. This strict requirement—along with provider reputation backchanneling—allows us to be confident in the quality of GDPx despite not having in-house expertise in every domain.
 Without naming any names, we dropped many potential partners (including some very prominent ones) who failed to pass our QA first try.
 Some domains also had multiple partners who wanted to be exclusive. In these cases, we ran a process to choose the provider with the better tasks. Sometimes multiple providers passed all our QA first try, which forced us to tiebreak on taste.
 The default time limit for a GDPx task is 8 hours, though some tasks had shorter time limits. We ran all models in their native harness when available (e.g. Claude Code for Opus 5.5, Codex for GPT 6 Astra, Antigravity for Gemini 4 Carbon, etc.). For models that don’t have a native harness, we default to OpenCode. Tasks use a mix of binary and partial grading depending on the domain. For the headline score, we report pass@1 across three attempts. All domains are weighted equally. For domains with multiple partners, each partner is weighted equally.
 A deep dive into every GDPx domain Being knowledgeable about RL is mostly sufficient for ensuring your benchmark tasks are fair, but it takes real domain expertise to guarantee tasks are interesting and realistic. Below, we’ll give a high-level overview of each partner and their task creation process. Each excerpt was largely written by the partners in their own words, with SemiAnalysis providing editorial support.
 Recursive self-improvement (RSI) 

 Source: GDPx 
 Our 10 recursive self-improvement (RSI) tasks were provided exclusively by Extrapolate . You can reach the team at founders@extrapolate-ai.com .
 Recursive self-improvement can mean different things depending on how it’s defined. We define RSI as an agent’s ability to autonomously build the next version of itself. Many believe this is the single most important capability to evaluate as frontier labs approach superintelligence.
 The main problem with existing RSI benchmarks is that they have a surprisingly narrow view of how frontier AI research actually works. Benchmarks like PostTrainBench and DeepRSI focus heavily on whether agents can train or fine-tune relatively small models on toy problems. While directionally correct, these benchmarks capture only a fraction of what it takes to build a frontier-grade model.
 Our approach is different. Rather than focusing exclusively on isolated model-training problems or novel algorithm discovery, we evaluate whether agents can autonomously perform the actual research workflows used inside frontier labs, from identifying reward hacking and debugging failed training runs to improving data quality, inference algorithms, and complex AI systems.
 Building a frontier model requires dozens of interconnected research workflows spanning pretraining, post-training, safety and alignment, evaluation design, data curation, and systems optimization. Much of the progress comes from thousands of iterative improvements across these systems, rather than a single revolutionary breakthrough.
 An agent capable of independently diagnosing training failures, identifying gaps in model capabilities, and developing better training recipes can accelerate the process of building its own successor. As these capabilities improve, the research process itself becomes increasingly automated, creating the feedback loop necessary for recursive self-improvement.
 Built by frontier AI researchers Extrapolate is a neolab for data focused on building the research environments and data flywheel needed to automate recursive self-improvement.
 The team brings firsthand experience from xAI, Scale AI, and Meta AI. Extrapolate’s CEO, Qasim Wani, kickstarted RSI efforts at xAI in February 2026 with Guodong Zhang (xAI cofounder) and was one of the main contributors to xAI MTS Eval , an internal RSI benchmark featured in the Grok 4.6 system card.
 Much of the research that advances frontier models never becomes public. The training failures, internal evaluations, and experimental decisions that determine how a model improves are rarely documented in papers.
 Turning real frontier research into RSI environments Extrapolate’s 10 GDPx tasks were built from research workflows encountered by its founding team while working at frontier AI labs. The benchmark spans RL debugging and reward hacking analysis, pretraining, post-training, data curation, KV-cache optimization, and improving complex AI systems.
 One of their main design principles is that real frontier research rarely starts from scratch. Researchers inherit existing codebases, model checkpoints, training logs, and experiments completed by other researchers. All our tasks inherit an already built complex codebase and logs the agent needs to comb through first before improving it further.
 Sample task: Debugging a broken large-scale RL run During Grok 4.5 development, Qasim and others spent two weeks debugging a single large-scale RL training run because Grok kept exploiting subtle failures in the training harness.
 Inspired by this experience, Extrapolate recreated a similar problem using a large-scale GRPO run containing approximately 1,000 rollouts on private RL tasks. The harness contained a subtle bug: when a rollout reached 32K tokens, it injected a message through a tool response instructing the model to “Stop exploring and write your final deliverables to disk now, then finish.” This unintentionally encouraged models to abandon their investigations and finalize incomplete solutions, degrading training performance. Not only does training on these degenerate rollouts result in a 3x lower mean reward compared to training on clean rollouts, it would also increase misaligned behavior since rollouts that ignored the harness instructions would obtain a higher reward; thus being incentivized by RL.
 Agents receive approximately 1,000 rollout traces comprising 21.2 million tokens of model behavior, alongside training rewards, evaluation results, and the historical harness code. They must investigate why training performance degraded and produce an evidence-backed diagnosis.
 The task is deceptively difficult. Changes in the types of tasks used during training make it difficult to tell whether the model is actually improving, creating several plausible explanations for the observed performance degradation. The real challenge is examining the underlying rollouts and harness code to distinguish these explanations from the actual root cause.

 Source: Extrapolate 
 Across 20 rollouts from Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon, and GLM 5.3, all four models struggled.

 Source: GDPx 
 Failure-mode analysis: Most agents correctly recognized that changes in the training task mixture made aggregate reward trends unreliable. However, they struggled to connect the harness instruction to the model’s dec

items.title: The Datacenter Backlash Goes Bipartisan: Next Week's Midterms and the 2028 Buildout
items.content:
The 2027 datacenter boom is already being built, and next week’s midterms won’t stop it now. Roughly three-quarters of the 33.8 GW due across our top 20 states is already under construction, which is why we remain comfortable with the global +50 GW year we laid out in our Oct. 16 article . The campuses are taking shape. The election will change the rules around them, but much of the 2027 pipeline already has a substantial head start.
 The fight is over 2028. Our model has 62.2 GW of US net additions that year, most of which hasn’t started construction. Much of it sits in states electing a governor on Nov. 3. This piece tracks the 13 states with the largest 2028 net additions in our model, setting aside Virginia and Mississippi, which don’t hold state elections this November. Together they account for 43.5 GW, or 70% of what we expect nationally, and 10 of the 13 elect a governor.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 That leaves a 2028 pipeline still working through approvals, power projects, and construction schedules as the rules change. In September, we argued that datacenter moratoriums weren’t killing the US buildout : of roughly 20 GW inside local restrictions, we estimated only 1.5 GW faced delay. Most exposed capacity already had protections or did not need the affected approval until after the pause expired. That broad conclusion has held up. What is changing is the reach of the restrictions given the growing anti-datacenter backlash.
 Three things have worsened since. Texas, the largest US market, froze Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) permits on Sept. 21 on top of the interconnection-queue audit begun Aug. 3, bringing onsite power into the hold. Oregon expanded its earlier state-land freeze to air and water-discharge permits on Oct. 9, through July 1, 2027. And midterm candidates have campaigned on more restrictive positions: nine of the 20 nominees want a pause on new construction and the other 11 want conditions; the split is about even by party. Both parties want developers to accept stricter conditions. The main difference is whether a developer can meet the new terms and keep building or must wait for the state to reopen approvals.
 The biggest risk to our buildout forecast right now is a prolonged permitting freeze at the TCEQ. Texas alone adds close to 30% of US GW in 2028. A few months of lost time in that market can move the national number. We already flagged to Datacenter Model subscribers which companies are most at risk from the current pause. The question now is how long the pause lasts.
 Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who is running for re-election in Texas, could reopen permitting once the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the state’s grid operator, finishes its audit and the Texas Water Development Board completes its water-use review. ERCOT is targeting Dec. 10 to file its report, which does not by itself reopen permitting. A restart around then would leave developers dealing with a relatively short interruption, which some projects can absorb within their schedules. The audit still has to lead to a decision to resume issuance, and each permit still needs approval.
 By contrast, Gina Hinojosa (D), his challenger, presents a more bearish approach: she would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for datacenters. The regular legislative session in Texas takes place from Jan. 12 to May 31, 2027. If approvals stay on hold throughout that session, the freeze would last about eight months from September. If reopening waits for the new rules to take effect in late summer, the freeze would last close to a year, or five to nine additional months compared with restarting in December. A deal or a special session might happen sooner. However, a campus racing toward delivery in 2027 may not have that much time to spare.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 This is the risk posed by the pro-moratorium candidates: a project cannot carry out work if it still requires an approval which the state has ceased to issue. If the candidate proposing a datacenter pause won in every state where one is running, those states would together contain roughly 30 GW of planned capacity scheduled for 2028. How much actually slips depends on the permits each project still needs and how long the pause lasts.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 We are less concerned with the candidates who support conditions only. Most of their demands change the price and terms of development. A developer can fund the grid upgrade, change the cooling design or negotiate the community agreement, and then move forward. That can be expensive and time-consuming, but it gives projects a route to approval. Several of the main conditions were already coming:
 Submitting thorough water-usage studies: manageable for many projects, but the answer depends on cooling design and the local water supply.
 Paying the infrastructure costs they create: we expect this to come anyway, with datacenter developers now offering credits toward household electricity bills. 
 More environmental transparency and dropping non-disclosure agreements (NDAs): Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google have already started down this path. 
 If the less restrictive candidates win, that exposure falls to 5.7 GW, mainly because Ohio and Oregon have proponents of a pause on both sides. That is a much smaller pipeline to test for delays. It would still be a tougher development environment: fewer tax breaks, more upfront commitments and less room to leave infrastructure costs with the utility’s other customers.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 According to race ratings and available polling as of Oct. 30, from multiple sources ( Cook Political Report , Multistate , and The New York Times ), the conditions-only candidate is favored in Texas, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and Iowa, and Georgia is a toss-up. Here we take candidates’ positions at face value. The extent of any delay will depend on whether these promises are turned into actual policy and whether the resulting pause hits a project at the wrong stage in its timeline.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 As noted in our September moratoriums article , these positions are overwhelmingly bipartisan now, with many campaigning on the following three points:
 Make datacenters pay their own grid costs (15 candidates)
 End the tax breaks (12 candidates)
 Limit or report water use (11 candidates)

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 Which states are the most impacted depends on which companies are building. We interviewed six current and former employees of hyperscalers, including people who worked at Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, and are involved in datacenter development. Several said that hyperscalers can afford to pay the higher costs of new rules and can more easily bring or pay for their own power.
 However, that doesn’t necessarily mean they will be able to deliver capacity on time. These projects still require their own permits and equipment. And having the money to pay for power transmission doesn’t make it available immediately. A moratorium can block any project that still needs approval, and it won’t be easy to shift development to another state: anywhere else would still require power, permits and construction schedules that can meet the same delivery timeline.
 We made the same point from the other direction in Stop Saying Half of 2026 US Datacenter Capacity Is Canceled . Many projects being described as 2026 delays were speculative announcements that never belonged in a credible 2026 forecast. Here, the task is to identify which real campuses still need the approval a candidate wants to stop. A governor’s campaign platform is the start of that work. The permit, power phase, and construction schedule tell us what happens to the megawatts.
 The Growing Anti-Datacenter Sentiment Shaping US Politics The datacenter backlash has moved faster than the industry expected. The AI boom has made these campuses visible, and candidates are tapping into concerns about jobs, noise, power rates and local resources. Those concerns now shape the terms on which developers can build.
 The local candidates we interviewed all said that NDAs that hide who developers are while they negotiate with local governments are a concern. “The public gets to know about all of this last,” said Rex Meyer (R), who is running for a seat on the Linn County Board of Supervisors in Iowa, which has datacenters and power projects being developed for Google and QTS within its borders. Meyer opposes the proposed Morgan Valley natural gas plant at its Fairfax site, which would support the nearby Google and QTS datacenters.
 Pam Marsh (D), who is up for re-election as a state representative in Oregon, said voter anxiety over AI is part of the problem. “We are starting to hear stories about people losing their jobs to AI. We’re looking at our kids, going: What can they train in? What should we be offering at our universities that will give people the best chance to make it in an AI world? And we don’t have clear answers to that yet.”
 Marsh is open to a brief pause on datacenter construction in her state while tougher policies are written but doesn’t support the three-year moratorium recently proposed by her fellow Democrats, which she sees as effectively a ban.
 In Georgia, Josh Tolbert (R), who is running for the Georgia Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, believes datacenters should pay their own way. “If a datacenter causes a cost, that datacenter should pay it. Existing customers’ bills should not go up because of datacenters. It is that simple,” he said.
 Development Risk at the State Level State and local authorities control many of the decisions that determine where and how quickly datacenters get built, including land use, permitting, and access to power. Federal policy also plays a role via its transmission rules, environmental permitting, infrastructure costs, and oversight.
 Politicians at the federal level have occasionally pushed for measures that would require state action. In Michigan, both Senate candidates, Mike Rogers (R) and Abdul El-Sayed (D), have called for datacenter moratoriums, but neither would have the power to enact one from the Senate.
 In our analysis, state elections, governors, legislatures, and utility commissions have the most influence over policy. Although governors can at times delay certain approvals, more extensive restrictions or changes to taxes generally have to go through legislation, as we explained in our September newsletter article on moratoriums .
 Governors can act quickly by halting permits an agency hasn’t issued, changing review priorities and directing agencies to impose conditions within their legal authority. Abbott’s TCEQ freeze and the environmental-permit hold imposed by Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek (D) show how quickly that can affect a schedule. Existing permits protect the work they authorize, but a campus can still need approval for its next power phase. Appointments also matter in Texas, Ohio and Pennsylvania; governors appoint utility commissioners, subject to Senate review. Ohio’s governor also shapes the Power Siting Board.
 Legislatures hold the money and the statute. The equipment sales-tax exemption is one of the biggest levers they wield, potentially worth billions of dollars per gigawatt, as it eliminates the sales tax on the servers, GPUs, networking gear, cooling systems, transformers and backup generators that fill a datacenter. Legislatures also write the statutory moratoria that outlast executive orders, which can be quickly repealed or reversed.
 Utility commissions decide what datacenters pay for power and the terms of service, including deposits, minimum bills, upgrade costs and exit fees. Commissioners are elected in Georgia, Arizona and Oklahoma and appointed in many other states. Staggered terms and confirmation requirements mean a governor’s victory doesn’t immediately change a commission’s majority. In states where the nation’s largest power transmission organization, PJM Interconnection, operates, governors don’t have much power over it.
 Across the largest datacenter markets with state elections this November, we ask whether Nov. 3 can change the relevant decision makers (governors, legislatures, and elected utility commissions), how much policy differs between the possible outcomes and how much capacity still depends on an affected decision. Local approvals remain a separate source of project risk. Our analysis focuses on state-level elections.

 Source: SemiAnalysis Datacenter Industry Model 
 We divided states into three tiers based on their unstarted capacity exposure in 2028 and how directly the Nov. 3 midterm results could change the policies affecting that capacity. In this analysis, we distinguish existing restrictions from changes the election could bring.
 Tier 1 includes states with large unstarted capacity exposure (>2 GW), where further restrictions are likely whoever wins. Texas, Ohio, and Arizona have restrictive candidates on both sides, while Georgia has a toss-up governor’s race and a Public Service Commission (PSC) majority on the ballot.
 Tier 2 includes states with meaningful unstarted capacity (1.5-2 GW) where additional restrictions depend on a change in political control, through Pennsylvania’s Senate race or a Democratic win in Oklahoma’s governor’s race.
 Tier 3 covers smaller unstarted capacity exposures (<1.5 GW), where more restrictive datacenter policies are highly likely: Illinois, Oregon and Iowa may face tighter policies whoever wins.
 We’re leaving out Indiana, Missouri, Wyoming, and West Virginia from these tiers. Indiana and Missouri have large Republican majorities and supportive governors staying in office. Wyoming is likely to retain Republican control of both branches, while West Virginia’s governor and dominant Republican legislature remain aligned on datacenter development
